title: Carbon and nitrogen: how the same atoms go round from the air to living beings and back

summary.text: A paddy plant stands in air that is nearly four-fifths nitrogen, yet the farmer still buys nitrogen fertiliser. Why can the plant not use it? In this lesson you will follow carbon and nitrogen atoms round their cycles, and test three compost bottles to see which rots best.
summary.art: A green paddy field under a wide sky, with a woman farmer carrying a white fertiliser bag on her head along the bund, and faint pairs of dots drawn in the air above the plants.

intro.hook: Air is nearly four-fifths nitrogen, and every plant needs nitrogen to grow. A plant stands in air all day and all night. So why do farmers buy nitrogen in bags?
intro.text: The nitrogen in the air is there, but plants have no way to take it in. In the air, nitrogen atoms hold on to each other in pairs, and a plant has no tool to pull a pair apart. A few kinds of bacteria have that tool. Almost all the nitrogen in your body passed through such bacteria, or through a factory, before it reached you. Carbon has its own path. A leaf takes carbon from the air, and your breath gives carbon back. In this lesson you follow both atoms all the way round. You also make compost, and find out why a good compost bin needs two kinds of waste.
intro.art: A girl standing barefoot on a paddy bund holding up a bean plant with soil on the roots, looking closely at small round lumps on the roots.

outcomes: By the end I can explain that living beings do not make or destroy atoms. The same atoms move between the air, water, soil, rocks and living bodies.
By the end I can follow a carbon atom round the carbon cycle, and name the steps that take carbon out of the air and the steps that put carbon back.
By the end I can explain why plants cannot use the nitrogen in the air, and name who changes that nitrogen into a form plants can use.
By the end I can follow a nitrogen atom round the nitrogen cycle, from the air to a plant, to an animal, to the soil and back to the air.
By the end I can run a fair compost test, and explain why decomposers work best with both carbon-rich 'browns' and nitrogen-rich 'greens'.
By the end I can explain how burning coal and oil and making fertiliser have changed the two cycles, and what has followed.
By the end I can tell a store from a flow, and say what a drawing or a game of a cycle leaves out.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny particles that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see. In living beings, atoms are never made and never destroyed. They only move and join up in new ways.
terms.example: A carbon atom in the sugar of a banana can leave your body in your breath an hour or two after you eat the banana.
terms.art: A banana, a child breathing out, and the same small black dot drawn inside the banana and then inside the breath.

terms.meaning: One kind of atom. Carbon atoms join in chains and rings, and these make the frame of sugar, starch, fat, wood, protein and every living body.
terms.example: The black part of burnt toast is mostly carbon that was in the bread.
terms.art: A slice of toast burnt black at one corner on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour and no smell. Each particle of this gas is one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms. This is the form in which carbon is found in the air.
terms.example: You breathe carbon dioxide out. The bubbles in soda water are carbon dioxide too.
terms.art: A glass of soda water with bubbles rising, next to a child breathing out on a cold morning.

terms.meaning: Another kind of atom. Every protein and every set of genes has nitrogen atoms in it. About 78 of every 100 particles of air are nitrogen gas.
terms.example: Dal is rich in protein, so dal is rich in nitrogen.
terms.art: A steel bowl of yellow toor dal, with the same bowl shown under a sky filled with tiny paired dots.

terms.meaning: The path that one kind of atom takes as it moves between the air, water, soil, rocks and living beings, and comes back to where it began.
terms.example: In the carbon cycle, a carbon atom can go from the air into a leaf, into a goat, and back into the air.
terms.art: A ring of four arrows joining a cloud, a leaf, a goat and a patch of soil.

terms.meaning: A place where many atoms of one kind stay for a time. The air, the sea, the soil, rocks and all living bodies are stores.
terms.example: A coal seam is a store of carbon. The carbon in coal has stayed there for hundreds of millions of years.
terms.art: A cut-away hillside showing a thick black layer of coal deep under green fields.

terms.meaning: The movement of atoms from one store to another. A cycle is made of stores joined by flows.
terms.example: When a leaf takes carbon dioxide from the air, carbon flows from the air into the plant.
terms.art: Two labelled boxes, Air and Plant, joined by one thick arrow.

terms.meaning: The way green plants and algae build sugar. They use carbon dioxide from the air, water, and the energy of light. They give off oxygen.
terms.example: A curry leaf plant on a balcony takes in carbon dioxide through tiny holes under each leaf.
terms.art: A curry leaf plant in a pot in sunlight, with an arrow of gas going into a leaf and another coming out.

terms.meaning: The way living cells get energy from food. The cell takes sugar apart using oxygen. The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. Plants, animals, fungi and most bacteria all respire.
terms.example: After you run, you breathe faster, because your muscle cells are respiring faster.
terms.art: A girl who has just finished running, hands on knees, breathing hard.

terms.meaning: Coal, oil or natural gas. These formed from living beings who were buried under mud and rock for millions of years. Burning a fossil fuel puts that old carbon into the air.
terms.example: The petrol in an auto and the coal burnt at a power station are fossil fuels.
terms.art: A yellow-and-black auto at a petrol pump, with a faint picture of ancient swamp plants inside the fuel hose.

terms.meaning: A kind of large particle that living bodies build and use for almost every job. Muscles, hair, enzymes and the red part of blood are proteins. Every protein contains nitrogen.
terms.example: Dal, milk, eggs, fish and groundnuts are foods rich in protein.
terms.art: A plate with dal, a glass of milk, an egg and a handful of groundnuts.

terms.meaning: Changing nitrogen gas from the air into a form that plants can take up. Certain bacteria do it. Lightning does a little, and fertiliser factories do a great deal.
terms.example: Bacteria living in the roots of a black gram plant fix nitrogen, and the plant uses it.
terms.art: A black gram plant with small round lumps on the roots and arrows of air going down into the soil towards them.

terms.meaning: A plant of the bean and pea family. The seeds grow in pods. Most legumes keep nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their roots.
terms.example: Black gram, green gram, toor dal, chana, groundnut, beans, peas and the touch-me-not plant are legumes.
terms.art: Open pods of black gram, green gram, groundnut and beans laid side by side.

terms.meaning: A small round lump on the root of a legume. The plant builds it as a home for nitrogen-fixing bacteria. A working nodule is pink or red inside.
terms.example: Dig up a groundnut plant gently, and you can see nodules like tiny beads on the roots.
terms.art: A close view of groundnut roots with pale round nodules, one cut open to show a pink inside.

terms.meaning: A gas with a sharp smell. Each particle is one nitrogen atom joined to three hydrogen atoms. In wet soil, ammonia turns into a form called ammonium, which stays in the soil.
terms.example: The sharp smell of a toilet that has not been cleaned is ammonia.
terms.art: A child holding their nose near a compost bin that is too wet.

terms.meaning: A form of nitrogen joined to oxygen. Nitrate dissolves in water, and plant roots take it up easily. Rain also washes it away easily.
terms.example: Bacteria in the soil turn ammonium into nitrate, and a paddy plant takes up both.
terms.art: A root in dark soil with small dots moving in the soil water towards the root hairs.

terms.meaning: Bacteria who live where there is little air, such as waterlogged soil. They use nitrate in place of oxygen, and give nitrogen gas back to the air.
terms.example: In a flooded paddy field, denitrifying bacteria send some of the fertiliser's nitrogen back into the air.
terms.art: A flooded paddy field in cross-section, with tiny bubbles rising from the mud to the air.

terms.meaning: Dark, crumbly matter that is left when decomposers have eaten plant and food waste. It holds nutrients and helps soil to hold water.
terms.example: Vegetable peels and dry leaves kept in a pot with air and a little water become compost in two to three months.
terms.art: Two hands holding dark crumbly compost over a terracotta pot.

terms.meaning: Two kinds of compost waste. Browns are dry and tough, with much carbon and little nitrogen. Greens are wet and soft, with more nitrogen.
terms.example: Dry leaves, torn newspaper and coconut fibre are browns. Vegetable peels, used tea leaves and old flowers are greens.
terms.art: Two heaps on a newspaper: dry brown leaves and paper on one side, wet vegetable peels and tea leaves on the other.

terms.meaning: Something added to soil to give plants nutrients. Compost and dung are fertilisers made by living beings. Urea is a nitrogen fertiliser made in a factory.
terms.example: A farmer in Thanjavur scatters white grains of urea on her paddy three or four weeks after planting.
terms.art: A woman farmer scattering white grains from a basket across a green paddy field.

explanations.concept: Atoms are kept: living beings only move them and join them in new ways
explanations.definition: A matter cycle is the path that one kind of atom takes between the air, water, soil, rocks and living beings. No living being makes atoms or destroys them.
explanations.description: When a seed grows into a tree, the tree's body has to come from somewhere. When a log rots, what the log was made of has to go somewhere. Chemists have weighed what goes in and what comes out of burning, rotting, growing and breathing. The weights always match. So every atom in a living body was somewhere else before, and will be somewhere else later. Almost no matter reaches the Earth from space or leaves it. The Earth has been using the same atoms for about four and a half billion years. Energy is different. Energy arrives from the Sun every day and leaves again as heat. This lesson follows two kinds of atom, carbon and nitrogen.
examples: The water you drink has been rain, river, sea and cloud many times before.
A carbon atom in your breakfast idli was in the air above a paddy field a few months ago.
In the project Bottle World, nothing goes into a sealed jar except light. The plant inside goes on living, because the atoms in the jar go round.
explanations.art: The Earth seen from space with a few arrows curving round inside the thin blue layer of air, and one arrow of sunlight arriving from outside.

explanations.concept: The fast carbon cycle: from the air to a leaf, to an eater, and back to the air
explanations.definition: In the fast carbon cycle, photosynthesis takes carbon out of the air and builds it into living bodies. Respiration, rotting and burning put the carbon back into the air.
explanations.description: A leaf takes in carbon dioxide through tiny holes. Using the energy of light, the leaf joins the carbon with water to build sugar. The plant builds starch, wood, oil and protein from that sugar. So most of the dry weight of a plant came out of the air. This surprises most people, because a plant seems to grow out of the soil. Soil gives the plant water and small amounts of minerals. When an animal eats the plant, the carbon passes into the animal. Every living cell respires. That means the cell takes sugar apart to get energy, and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. Decomposers do the same with dead leaves and bodies. A carbon atom can go round this path in less than a year.
examples: About half of the dry weight of wood is carbon, and all of that carbon came from the air.
About 18 of every 100 grams of your body is carbon. You ate all of it.
When a person becomes thinner, most of the lost fat leaves the body as carbon dioxide in the breath.
explanations.art: A ring drawn on a notebook page: air to a paddy leaf, paddy grain to a plate of idli, a child eating, and the child's breath going back to the air.

explanations.concept: Stores and flows: where carbon stays, and for how long
explanations.definition: A store is a place where carbon stays for a time. A flow is the movement of carbon from one store to another. A cycle is a set of stores joined by flows.
explanations.description: The Earth's carbon is in five main stores. They are the air, living beings, the soil, the sea and rocks. The stores are very different in size. The air is one of the smaller stores, though it is the store that every plant feeds from. All the plants on land together hold about half as much carbon as the air. The soil holds more than the air and all the plants together, as dead matter that decomposers have not finished eating. The sea holds many times more than the air, dissolved in the water. Rocks hold far more than all the others together. A carbon atom stays in each store for a different time. It may stay a few years in the air, hundreds of years in the deep sea, and millions of years in a rock.
examples: In the game Carbon Journey, you leave the Air station on most throws, but you leave the Rock station only on a six.
A fallen teak leaf in a Kerala forest rots within a year. The carbon in a teak door can stay there for two hundred years.
The soil of a forest floor is dark because of the carbon stored in it.
explanations.art: Five labelled jars of very different sizes in a row: a small one for air, a smaller one for plants, a medium one for soil, a large one for the sea and a huge drum for rock.

explanations.concept: The slow carbon cycle: shells, limestone, coal and volcanoes
explanations.definition: In the slow carbon cycle, carbon is locked into rock and fossil fuel for millions of years, and comes back to the air through volcanoes and the slow wearing away of rock.
explanations.description: Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in the sea. Many sea beings, such as snails, clams, corals and some tiny algae, take dissolved carbon and build shells from it. When they die, the shells sink and pile up on the sea floor. Over millions of years the piles are pressed into a rock called limestone. Some carbon is locked away in another way. In swamps and on sea floors, dead plants and algae are sometimes buried under mud before decomposers can eat them. Heat and pressure slowly turn them into coal, oil and gas. Left alone, this carbon comes back to the air very slowly. Rock is pushed down and melted deep in the Earth, and volcanoes let the carbon dioxide out. One full round can take more than a hundred million years.
examples: The coal of Singareni in Telangana and Jharia in Jharkhand formed from forests that grew more than 250 million years ago.
A marble floor tile, a piece of limestone and an eggshell are all made of the same carbon-holding mineral as sea shells.
In the experiment Sour Air, carbon dioxide went into water in a few minutes. The sea takes it in the same way.
explanations.art: A cut-away picture of the sea floor with shells piling up at the bottom, layers of pale limestone below them, and a volcano on land letting out gas.

explanations.concept: What burning coal, oil and gas does to the carbon cycle
explanations.definition: Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from rock to the air many times faster than volcanoes do. So the amount of carbon dioxide in the air is rising.
explanations.description: In 1958 an American scientist, Charles David Keeling, began to measure the carbon dioxide in clean air on Mauna Loa, a mountain in Hawaii. The measuring has gone on ever since. In 1960 there were about 317 particles of carbon dioxide in every million particles of air. In 2025 there were about 427. The line also goes down a little every northern summer and up every winter. In summer the forests of the northern lands are in leaf, and they take in more carbon than living beings give out. Each year people now add about 40 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide to the air. About half of it stays in the air. The sea takes up about a quarter, and plants and soil on land take up the rest. Carbon dioxide lets sunlight in and slows the escape of heat, so the Earth is slowly warming.
examples: In the activity Read the Keeling Curve, you plot the real numbers and see that the line climbs faster now than in the 1960s.
In 1856 an American scientist, Eunice Foote, put glass tubes of different gases in sunlight. The tube of carbon dioxide grew warmest and stayed warm longest.
The sea has taken up so much carbon dioxide that sea water is now slightly less alkaline than it was 200 years ago.
explanations.art: A rising zigzag line on a graph, with a small observatory hut on a bare volcanic mountain drawn beside it.

explanations.concept: Nitrogen: plenty in the air, but out of reach
explanations.definition: Nitrogen gas is made of pairs of nitrogen atoms. The two atoms in a pair hold each other so strongly that plants and animals cannot pull them apart.
explanations.description: Every living being needs nitrogen. Proteins are built from it, and so are genes. About 3 of every 100 grams of your body is nitrogen. About 78 of every 100 particles of air are nitrogen gas. So nitrogen seems to be the easiest thing in the world to get. But in the air, each nitrogen atom is joined to one other nitrogen atom by one of the strongest joins in nature. You breathe nitrogen in and breathe all of it out again, unchanged. A plant's leaves are bathed in nitrogen, and the plant can use none of it. A plant takes up nitrogen mainly when a nitrogen atom is joined to hydrogen, as ammonium, or to oxygen, as nitrate. That is why a crop can turn yellow for want of nitrogen while standing in air that is mostly nitrogen.
examples: A paddy plant short of nitrogen has pale yellow older leaves and stays small.
A packet of chips is filled with nitrogen gas to keep the chips crisp. The gas is used because it hardly reacts with anything.
In Browns, Greens or Both, the bottle of paper and dry leaves stood in air full of nitrogen and still rotted slowly.
explanations.art: A pale yellow paddy plant in the middle of a picture crowded with tiny pairs of dots, none of them entering the plant.

explanations.concept: The nitrogen fixers: who can open the pair
explanations.definition: Nitrogen fixing means changing nitrogen gas into ammonia, a form that living beings can use. Certain bacteria do it. Lightning and fertiliser factories do it too.
explanations.description: Some kinds of bacteria make an enzyme that can pull a pair of nitrogen atoms apart and join each atom to hydrogen. An enzyme is a protein that does one job on one kind of particle. Some of these bacteria live free in soil and water. Some live inside the roots of legumes, such as black gram, groundnut and beans. The plant builds a small round home for them, called a root nodule, and feeds them sugar. The bacteria give the plant nitrogen. A working nodule is pink inside. The colour comes from a red protein, a relative of the one in our blood, which carries oxygen to the bacteria in small, safe amounts. Too much oxygen stops the enzyme. In flooded paddy fields, blue-green bacteria fix nitrogen in the water. Lightning is hot enough to join nitrogen to oxygen, but it fixes only a small share.
examples: In 1939 the Indian scientist P. K. De showed that blue-green bacteria fix nitrogen in the water of paddy fields. This helps to explain how the same fields could grow rice for centuries.

Azolla is a tiny floating fern with nitrogen-fixing bacteria living inside the leaves. Farmers in Vietnam and China have grown azolla in paddy water for centuries, and some Indian farmers grow it today.
In 2024 scientists reported a sea alga with a nitrogen-fixing part inside each cell. The part was once a free bacterium.
explanations.art: A black gram root with round nodules, one cut in half and pink inside, and a magnified circle showing rod-shaped bacteria packed within.

explanations.concept: Legumes and bacteria signal to each other and choose
explanations.definition: A legume and nitrogen-fixing bacteria find each other by sending chemical signals through the soil. Each answers only the right partner.
explanations.description: A legume root short of nitrogen lets certain chemicals out into the soil. Bacteria of the right kind sense them, swim towards the root and send a signal of their own back. When the root hair senses that reply, the root hair curls round the bacteria and lets them in. The plant then builds a nodule around them. The plant goes on checking. In a test with soya bean plants in 2003, scientists stopped the bacteria in some nodules from fixing nitrogen. The plants gave those nodules less oxygen, and the bacteria in them multiplied far less. So the plant senses which nodules are giving nitrogen, and decides which ones to keep feeding. Plants and bacteria sense, signal and decide. Some scientists prefer to call all of this automatic chemistry.
examples: A black gram plant growing in soil rich in nitrogen makes few nodules. The plant does not pay sugar for nitrogen they can get freely.
Each kind of legume lets in only certain kinds of bacteria. The bacteria of a pea plant are turned away by a soya bean.
In the story The Kiln Field, the plants in a new field had no nodules, because the right bacteria were not in that soil.

perspectives.who: Toby Kiers, Ford Denison and their team, who did the soya bean test
perspectives.explanation: The plant acts like a careful trader, rewarding partners who give nitrogen and cutting off partners who do not.
No choosing is needed to explain this. A nodule that makes less nitrogen sets off chemical changes that lower the oxygen reaching it.

explanations.art: A magnified root hair curling round a cluster of small rod-shaped bacteria, with tiny dots drifting both ways between the root and the bacteria.

explanations.concept: The nitrogen cycle, step by step
explanations.definition: In the nitrogen cycle, bacteria fix nitrogen from the air, plants and animals use it, decomposers free it from dead matter, and other bacteria return it to the air.
explanations.description: Step one is fixing. Bacteria change nitrogen gas into ammonia, which becomes ammonium in wet soil. Step two is uptake. Plant roots take up the ammonium and build proteins. Animals get their nitrogen by eating plants, or by eating animals who ate plants. Step three is the return to the soil. Animals pass out spare nitrogen in urine, and all living beings die. Decomposers eat the dead matter and the wastes, and set the nitrogen free as ammonium again. Step four is nitrifying. Certain soil bacteria get their energy by changing ammonium into nitrate. Roots take up nitrate even more easily. Step five closes the ring. In wet soil with little air, denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen and give off nitrogen gas. Every step except the eating is done by microbes, which means living beings too small to see. Most of them are bacteria.
examples: In the activity The Nitrogen Relay, a ball marked N passes round six stations. Three of the six are microbes.
Cow urine and dung have been put on Indian fields for thousands of years. Decomposers free their nitrogen for the crop.
Rain washes nitrate out of bare soil, because nitrate dissolves in water and does not stick to soil grains.
explanations.art: A ring of five labelled arrows around a field: air to nodule, soil to root, plant to cow, dung to soil, and wet mud back to air.

explanations.concept: Compost: giving decomposers a balanced meal
explanations.definition: Composting is keeping plant and food waste so that decomposers can eat it with enough air and water. Decomposers need carbon for energy and nitrogen to build their bodies.
explanations.description: Decomposers are living beings, and their bodies are built of protein like ours. So they need nitrogen as well as carbon. Dry leaves, paper and straw are mostly carbon. Gardeners call them browns. Vegetable peels, tea leaves and fresh grass hold more nitrogen and much more water. Gardeners call them greens. With only browns, the decomposers have plenty of energy food and too little nitrogen to multiply, so the heap rots very slowly. With only greens, the heap packs down wet and the air cannot get in. Bacteria who live without air take over and make bad smells. There is also more nitrogen than the decomposers can use, and the spare nitrogen leaves as ammonia gas. A mix of about two parts browns to one part greens gives them both foods, with air between the pieces. A large heap of such a mix grows hot, because so many decomposers are respiring.
examples: In Browns, Greens or Both, you test the three mixes side by side and measure how far each one sinks.

From 1924 to 1931, at Indore, Albert Howard and the chemist Yeshwant Wad worked out a way of composting in layers. It is still called the Indore method, and it drew on the old practice of farmers in India and China. Gabrielle Howard, a plant scientist, had worked beside Albert on Indian crops for 25 years.
The inside of a large compost heap can reach 55 to 65 degrees Celsius, too hot to keep your hand in.
explanations.art: A cut-away terracotta compost pot showing layers of dry leaves and vegetable peels, with air holes in the sides and dark compost at the bottom.

explanations.concept: How people have changed the nitrogen cycle
explanations.definition: Factories now fix nitrogen from the air to make fertiliser. People fix about as much nitrogen each year as all natural fixing on land and in the sea together.
explanations.description: In 1908 the German chemist Fritz Haber patented a way to join nitrogen from the air with hydrogen, using great heat and pressure. Carl Bosch turned it into a factory process. The ammonia is made into fertilisers such as urea. Crops fed with it yield far more grain. One careful estimate says that food grown with this nitrogen feeds nearly half the people alive. But a crop takes up only part of the fertiliser. Rain washes some of the rest into streams and lakes. There it feeds algae, tiny green beings who live in water. They multiply until the water turns green. When they die, decomposers use up the oxygen in the water, and fish die. Soil bacteria also turn some of the spare nitrogen into nitrous oxide, a gas that warms the Earth. Farmers lose less nitrogen when they give smaller amounts at the right time.
examples: Since 2015, all urea made in India for farming is coated with neem oil. The neem slows the soil bacteria who change urea's nitrogen into nitrate, so less is washed away.
Lakes in many Indian cities turn green with algae or fill with water hyacinth, because sewage and field water bring them nitrogen and other nutrients.
In the challenge Keep It in the Field, you test ways to stop rain from carrying fertiliser off a slope of soil.
explanations.art: A split picture: on one side a tall crop of paddy beside an empty fertiliser bag, on the other a pond turned bright green with a dead fish at the edge.

explanations.concept: Your body is part of both cycles
explanations.definition: The atoms of your body are not fixed in place. Carbon and nitrogen atoms enter with food, stay for a time, and leave in breath, urine and shed cells.
explanations.description: You look the same from month to month, but your body is being rebuilt all the time. Scientists found a clever way to measure this. In the 1950s and early 1960s, nuclear bombs were tested in the open air. The tests added a rare, heavier kind of carbon atom to the air, and plants took it in. Everyone alive then ate it. After most of these tests stopped in 1963, the amount in the air fell year by year. So the amount of this carbon in a cell shows the year when that cell was made. In 2005 Kirsty Spalding, Jonas Frisén and their team in Sweden used this to date human cells. Most cells turned out to be much younger than the person. About a tenth of your fat cells are replaced each year. The nerve cells in the outer layer of the brain are as old as you are.
examples: Spare nitrogen leaves your body as urea in urine. That is the same substance that farmers buy as fertiliser.
The outer layer of your skin is shed and replaced all the time. The dust in a house contains shed skin.
The carbon you breathe out today can be in a leaf of a street tree by next week.
explanations.art: A child's outline filled with small dots, some dots arriving from a plate of food and others leaving in breath, with the outline staying the same.

explanations.concept: Do living beings keep the cycles steady?
explanations.description: The amount of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen in the air has stayed within limits that suit life for hundreds of millions of years. Living beings make and use all three gases. In the 1970s James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed that living beings, taken all together, keep the air and the climate suitable for life. They called this the Gaia idea, after a Greek name for the Earth. Other scientists objected strongly. Scientists still argue about how far the idea is true. Everyone agrees that living beings shape the air. They disagree about whether anything keeps it steady.
examples: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by photosynthesis. Before there were living beings who could photosynthesise, the air had almost none.
About 2.4 billion years ago, blue-green bacteria filled the air with oxygen. Oxygen was a poison to many of the beings alive then, and scientists think many kinds died out.
Today one kind of living being, humans, is changing the amount of carbon dioxide in the air within a few lifetimes.

perspectives.who: James Lovelock, a British chemist, and Lynn Margulis, an American biologist
perspectives.explanation: The living beings of the Earth and their surroundings act together as one system. When something shifts, living beings respond in ways that tend to bring it back.

perspectives.who: Ford Doolittle, a Canadian biologist, writing in 1981
perspectives.explanation: No being works for the good of the planet. Each bacterium takes what feeds them now. The cycles are a side effect, and nothing promises that they will stay steady.
Some feedbacks steady the Earth and some make changes bigger. Each one has to be measured. Life has both steadied the planet and upset it.

explanations.art: The Earth drawn as a round garden seen from above, with two scientists standing on either side of it, one pointing to the whole and one to a single small plant.

agreed.text: Living beings do not make or destroy atoms. Growing, eating, breathing, rotting and burning only move atoms and join them in new ways.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have weighed everything that goes into these changes and everything that comes out, in closed containers. The total weight stays the same every time.

agreed.text: Most of the dry weight of a plant is built from carbon dioxide and water, not from soil.
agreed.evidence: Scientists gave plants carbon dioxide made with a rare, heavier kind of carbon atom. Soon afterwards they found that carbon in the plants' sugar.

agreed.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air has risen by about a third since 1960, and the extra carbon comes mainly from fossil fuels.
agreed.evidence: Measurements on Mauna Loa show about 317 parts in a million in 1960 and about 427 in 2025. Air trapped in old ice shows that the level was far lower before factories. The extra carbon also lacks the rare kind of carbon atom that slowly disappears with great age, as coal and oil do.

agreed.text: Plants and animals cannot fix nitrogen by themselves. In nature, almost all nitrogen fixing is done by certain microbes.
agreed.evidence: In the 1880s Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth grew peas in clean sand with no nitrogen. The peas grew well only when water from ordinary soil was added, and only then did nodules form on the roots.

agreed.text: People now fix about as much nitrogen each year as all the natural fixing on land and in the sea together.
agreed.evidence: A study of the whole nitrogen cycle in 2013 put the yearly total at about 413 million tonnes of nitrogen. About 210 million tonnes of that came from fertiliser factories, crops grown for their nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and engines.

agreed.text: Decomposers need both carbon and nitrogen, and compost forms fastest when the waste has both, with air and water.
agreed.evidence: Compost makers have tested many mixes. Heaps of dry leaves alone or wet scraps alone rot slowly or go sour. Your own test with three bottles shows the same.

challenging.claim: A plant's body is made from the soil the plant grows in.
challenging.who: A very common belief, held by most children and many adults
challenging.for: A plant grows out of the soil and dies without it. Plants in poor soil stay small. Farmers add things to the soil to make crops grow.
challenging.against: A large tree weighs many tonnes, yet the soil level under the tree does not sink. Most of the dry weight of a plant is carbon and oxygen taken from the air as carbon dioxide, with hydrogen from water. Soil gives water, nitrogen and minerals. These are needed, but they are a small part of the weight.
challenging.context: This card is about the common belief that plants are built out of soil.

challenging.claim: When we breathe out, we add to the warming of the Earth.
challenging.who: A worry that many children have once they learn that carbon dioxide warms the Earth
challenging.for: Breath does contain carbon dioxide. Eight billion people and billions of other animals breathe out all day.
challenging.against: The carbon in your breath came from your food. Your food took that carbon out of the air a few months earlier. So breathing puts back what plants took out, and the amount in the air stays the same. The carbon in coal and oil has been out of the air for millions of years. Burning them adds carbon that the air did not have.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the carbon dioxide in our breath changes the air the way burning coal does.

challenging.claim: Factory fertiliser harms the land, and compost is always better.
challenging.for: Compost adds carbon to the soil, which feeds soil life and helps the soil hold water. Compost lets its nitrogen out slowly, so less is washed away. Factory fertiliser used carelessly pollutes water and air.
challenging.against: A root takes up the same ammonium and nitrate whether they came from compost or from a factory. There is not nearly enough compost and dung to grow food for eight billion people. Careful use of small amounts of factory fertiliser, together with compost, wastes the least.
challenging.context: This card is about whether nitrogen from a factory is worse for the land than nitrogen from compost.

challenging.claim: Growing dal always leaves the soil richer in nitrogen.
challenging.for: Legumes with working nodules take nitrogen from the air. Crops grown after a legume often do better.
challenging.against: Much of the nitrogen a dal plant fixes goes into the seeds, and the seeds are taken away and eaten. If the stems and roots are also removed, the soil may gain little. The soil gains most when the whole plant is ploughed back in. And a legume without the right bacteria fixes nothing.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a crop of dal always adds nitrogen to a field.

challenging.claim: Planting enough trees can cancel the carbon from burning coal and oil.
challenging.for: A growing tree takes carbon out of the air and stores it in wood for many years. Forests also shelter many living beings.
challenging.against: A tree holds carbon for decades or a few centuries, and gives it back when the tree burns or rots. Coal and oil held their carbon for millions of years. There is not enough spare land to grow trees for all the carbon that people burn. Most scientists say that trees help, and that burning less is still needed.
challenging.context: This card is about whether planting trees can make up for burning fossil fuels.

challenging.claim: Spreading crushed rock on farm fields can take carbon dioxide out of the air.
challenging.who: Some scientists and companies. One of them, working with small farmers in India, won a large world prize for carbon removal in 2025
challenging.for: Rain with carbon dioxide dissolved in it slowly wears rock away, and the carbon ends up locked in the sea. This is part of the slow carbon cycle. Crushing the rock gives the rain far more surface to work on, so it happens faster.
challenging.against: It is hard to measure how much carbon a field has really taken up. Digging, crushing and carrying rock burns fuel. Nobody yet knows how well it works over many years and many kinds of soil.
challenging.context: This card is about a new idea for speeding up one slow step of the carbon cycle.

big_questions.q: A plant stands in air full of nitrogen and still goes short of it. What else do people have all around them and still cannot use?
big_questions.hint: Think of sea water for a thirsty sailor, or a library for someone who has not learned to read.

big_questions.q: Some carbon atoms in your body were once in a dinosaur, a fern or a rock. So in what way is your body yours?
big_questions.hint: Your atoms change, but your shape and your memories stay. Which of these is 'you'?

big_questions.q: If the same atoms keep going round, why do we need the Sun every single day?
big_questions.hint: Atoms can be used again. Can the energy that leaves your body as heat be used again?

big_questions.q: Bacteria too small to see do most of the steps in the nitrogen cycle. Who matters more to a forest, the tiger or the bacteria?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to the forest in ten years without each of them?

big_questions.q: Carbon from coal was out of the air for 250 million years. Why does putting it back in 200 years cause trouble?
big_questions.hint: Think about flows. What happens to a bucket when water runs in faster than it runs out?

big_questions.q: Factory fertiliser feeds nearly half the world, and it also pollutes lakes and air. How should people decide how much to use?
big_questions.hint: Who gains and who loses when a farmer uses more? Who gains and who loses when she uses less?

story.title: The Kiln Field
story.note: The farming in this story is real. In the Cauvery delta of Tamil Nadu, farmers throw ulundu (black gram) seed into standing paddy 5 to 10 days before the harvest. The ulundu grows on the water left in the mud. Selling the top layer of a field to a brick kiln is also real. Working root nodules are pink inside. Farm scientists in Tamil Nadu advise coating the seed with a packet of the right bacteria, using cooled rice kanji to make it stick. Before such packets were sold, moving soil from an old legume field to a new one was a known way to carry the bacteria. Thenmozhi, her family, the officer and what happened in their two fields are made up.
text: Thenmozhi's family had two fields that year. The old field had been her grandmother's, and her great-grandmother's before that. The new one her mother had taken on rent during the rains, cheaply, and everybody called it the kiln field. Its last owner had sold the top of its soil, a foot deep, to a brick kiln.

In January, a week before the paddy was cut, her uncle Selvam had walked through both fields throwing ulundu seed into the standing crop. Ulundu is black gram, the dal that goes into idli and vadai. It was the same seed from the same sack, thrown by the same hand on the same morning. The seeds sank into the wet mud between the paddy stalks. When the paddy was harvested, the ulundu was already up.

Now it was the last week of February. In the old field the ulundu stood as high as Thenmozhi's shin, and the leaves were a dark, even green. In the kiln field the plants were half that height, and yellow.
"Bad seed," said Selvam Mama.
"It is the same seed," said Thenmozhi's mother.
"Then the field wants urea. One bag."
"With what money? The ulundu is the money."
Paatti, her grandmother, said nothing. She was looking at the yellow field the way she looked at a child with a fever.

Thenmozhi sat on the bund between the two fields with her feet in the stubble. Same seed. Same sun. Same water too, because nobody watered ulundu. The plants lived on what the paddy had left behind in the mud. She was ten, and she liked a problem with only one loose end. Whatever was different, it was not above the ground. So it had to be below.

She borrowed Paatti's weeding blade. In the old field she dug in a circle round one plant and lifted the plant out with the soil still on, the way you lift a seedling you mean to keep. She did the same in the kiln field. Then she carried both plants to the water channel and let the water take the mud off the roots slowly.

The yellow plant's roots were thin white threads, and that was all. The green plant's roots had beads on them. The beads were round and pale, the size of sago pearls. There were a dozen or more, stuck along the threads.
"Mama! The good one is sick. Look, boils."
Selvam Mama came and looked and frowned. "Root worms," he said. "Then both fields are finished."

"Give me that," said Paatti. She took the green plant, pinched off one bead and split it with her thumbnail. Inside, the bead was pink, like the flesh of a guava. "This is no sickness. A plant with these is a plant who is eating well. When I was a girl we looked for them. Pink inside meant a good crop."
"Then why has the kiln field none?" asked Thenmozhi.

Paatti was quiet for a while. "When I came here as a bride, your great-grandmother opened new land beyond the canal. Before the first ulundu, she made me carry three baskets of earth from this field and scatter them over that one. I thought it was a custom, like breaking a coconut. I asked her why. She said, 'That field has not met ulundu yet. Somebody must introduce them.'"

Thenmozhi turned the pink bead over on her palm. There was a page in her science book that she had read without much interest. It said that plants of the bean family keep bacteria in small lumps on their roots. The bacteria take nitrogen from the air, which no plant can do alone, and give it to the plant. The plant gives them sugar.
So the beads were not exactly part of the plant. They were rooms, and somebody lived in them. And that somebody had to come from somewhere.
"They live in the soil," she said slowly. "In old ulundu soil. And the top of the kiln field..."
"Went to the kiln," said her mother.
"They baked them," said Thenmozhi. "They are inside somebody's wall."

It was late in the season, and Paatti said so. A plant four weeks old has already settled most of what they will become. But Thenmozhi wanted to know, and wanting to know costs less than urea. She filled a bucket with soil from the old field, taken from close around the roots. She stirred it into water until it was as thin as buttermilk. Then she poured it along two rows of the kiln field, right at the feet of the plants. She pushed a stick into the bund to mark the place. The rest of the field she left alone.

For ten days nothing happened, and Selvam Mama enjoyed saying so. In the third week he stopped saying it. The two rows by the stick were not dark green. But they were greener than their neighbours, the way one washed shirt shows on a line of unwashed ones. Thenmozhi dug up a plant from the two rows. She had to look hard. Near the top of the root there were five small beads. She split one. It was pink.
She did not say anything to Mama. She only held it where he could see.

The kiln field gave less than a third of what the old field gave that year. In April a woman from the research station at Aduthurai came through the village, and Thenmozhi's mother told her the story. The officer laughed, though kindly, and took a small packet from her bag. Inside was a black powder.
"Your bucket, in a packet," she said. "The same bacteria, grown and counted. Mix it with cooled rice kanji so that it sticks. Roll the seed in it, dry the seed in the shade, and sow the same day."

The next January, Thenmozhi rolled the seed herself on a palm-leaf mat, a sackful, until every seed was coated grey. She added one handful of earth from the old field. She told herself it was not for luck. Then Selvam Mama walked into the standing paddy of the kiln field and threw.

In the last week of February she went out alone with the weeding blade. The kiln field was green from bund to bund. She dug up one plant anyway, washed the roots in the channel and counted the beads. She did not need to split one. But she did.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Thenmozhi sees that the beads on the roots are homes for bacteria, and that the bacteria must already be in the soil. A black gram plant cannot take nitrogen from the air alone. Bacteria in the root nodules do it, and the plant feeds them sugar. The kiln field had lost its top soil, and the bacteria with it. So the same seed under the same sky went short of nitrogen. Her two marked rows were a fair test: the same field, with one thing changed.
ask: Both fields had the same seed, sun and water. Why did Thenmozhi decide to look under the ground?
Why were the plants in the kiln field yellow, when the air above them was full of nitrogen?
Why did she pour the muddy water on only two rows and leave the rest alone?
What does the plant give the bacteria, and what do the bacteria give the plant?
The officer's packet and Paatti's baskets of earth did the same job. What was the job?

games.title: Carbon Journey
games.context: This is a dice game about the carbon cycle. You are one carbon atom. A die decides where you go next: the air, a plant, an animal, the soil, the sea, rock or coal. You find out which stores you leave quickly and which ones hold you.

printables.title: 7 stations to write on 7 sheets of paper and lay in a ring
7 two-sided station cards (the dice table is on the back)

items.f: AIR. You are in a particle of carbon dioxide, drifting in the air.
items.b: 1, 2 or 3: a leaf takes you in. Go to Plant. 4 or 5: you dissolve in the sea. Go to Sea Water. 6: you stay in the Air.

items.f: PLANT. A leaf has built you into sugar.
items.b: 1 or 2: the plant respires. Go to Air. 3: an animal eats the plant. Go to Animal. 4 or 5: a leaf falls. Go to Soil. 6: you are built into wood. Stay in Plant.

items.f: ANIMAL. You are part of an animal's body or food.
items.b: 1, 2, 3 or 4: the animal breathes you out. Go to Air. 5 or 6: you leave in dung, or the animal dies. Go to Soil.

items.f: SOIL. You are in a dead leaf, in dung or in dark soil.
items.b: 1, 2 or 3: a decomposer eats you and breathes you out. Go to Air. 4 or 5: you stay in the dark part of the soil. 6: mud buries you deep. Go to Coal and Oil.

items.f: SEA WATER. You are dissolved in the sea.
items.b: 1 or 2: you escape back to the Air. 3 or 4: a sea snail builds you into a shell. Go to Shell and Rock. 5 or 6: you sink into deep water. Stay in Sea Water.

items.f: SHELL AND ROCK. You are in a shell on the sea floor, slowly turning into limestone.
items.b: 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: you stay in the rock. 6: a volcano lets you out. Go to Air.

items.f: COAL AND OIL. You are buried deep under the ground.
items.b: 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: you stay underground. 6: you are dug up and burnt. Go to Air.

printables.title: A journey sheet for each player, to rule on paper
items: The station I am in after this throw

rules: Lay the 7 station sheets in a ring on the floor or a table. Put each station card on its sheet, dice table up.
Each player is one carbon atom. Use a coin or a button as your atom. Everyone starts in the Air.
On your turn, throw the die. Read the dice table of the station you are in, and move or stay as it says.
Say aloud what happened to you, for example 'A leaf took me in.' Write the station on your journey sheet.
The first player to have been in 5 different stations wins the race.
Then everyone goes on to 20 throws, and counts how many throws they spent in each station.
Playing alone: count how many throws you need to visit 5 stations. Play again and try to beat it.

setup.art: Seven sheets of paper laid in a ring on a floor, each with a station name in large letters and a small card on top.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 7 stations in a ring. Put a station card on each.

setup.art: A child's hand throwing a die beside a coin that sits on the sheet marked Air.
setup.caption: 2. Start in the Air. Throw the die and read that station's table.

setup.art: A coin being moved from the Air sheet to the Plant sheet, with a child writing 'Plant' on a ruled journey sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Move or stay. Say what happened, and write the station down.

flow.do: 1. Write the 7 station names on 7 sheets of paper. 2. Copy or cut out the 7 station cards. 3. Lay the sheets in a ring with a card on each. 4. Rule a journey sheet with 20 rows for each player.
flow.say: In this game you are one carbon atom. A carbon atom never wears out. It only moves from place to place. Where do you think you will spend the most time?
flow.kid: Write the 7 station names on 7 sheets. Lay them in a ring. Put a card on each. You are one carbon atom. Where will you spend the most time? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Carbon Journey. Here you lay out the seven stations and guess where a carbon atom spends the most time.

flow.do: 1. Everyone puts a coin on Air. 2. Take turns to throw the die. 3. Read the table for your station and move or stay. 4. Say what happened and write the station down. 5. This practice round ends when someone has been in 5 different stations.
flow.say: Throw the die and read your table. What just happened to you? Which living being or which place are you part of now?
flow.kid: Put your coin on Air. Throw the die. Read the table for your station. Move or stay. Say what happened. Write the station down. The round ends when someone has visited 5 stations.

ask.q: Which step took you out of the air? Which steps put you back?
good: A leaf took me out of the air. That is photosynthesis.
Breathing, rotting and burning put me back.

flow.parent: Ask for the real name of each move as it happens. A leaf taking carbon in is photosynthesis. A plant, an animal or a decomposer giving carbon out is respiration.
flow.context: This is the race in Carbon Journey. Here each player throws the die, moves between stations and says what happened to their carbon atom.

flow.do: 1. Start again on Air. Everyone goes on until they have made 20 throws. 2. Count how many throws you spent in each station. 3. Compare your counts. 4. Ask which stations were quick to leave and which were slow.
flow.say: Count your throws in each station. Where did you get stuck? Why is it hard to leave that station?
flow.kid: Start again on Air. Make 20 throws. Count your throws in each station. Where did you get stuck? Why was it hard to leave?

ask.q: Did anyone reach Shell and Rock or Coal and Oil? What happened there?
good: I stayed for many throws, because only a six lets you out.
Nobody reached them, because the way in is rare too.

flow.parent: The die makes rock look far quicker than it is. A real carbon atom can stay in limestone for more than a hundred million years. The game shows only which stores are quick and which are slow.

check.q: In which of these stores does a carbon atom usually stay the longest?
check.why: Carbon in rock comes out only through volcanoes or very slow wearing away, over millions of years. Carbon in an animal is breathed out within hours or years. Choosing the air is a fair guess, because the air is so big. But leaves and the sea take carbon out of the air within a few years.

flow.context: This step of Carbon Journey comes after the race. Here you count how long your carbon atom stayed in each station, and find the slow ones.

flow.do: 1. Put 6 coins on Coal and Oil. 2. Throw the die once for each coin. A coin goes to Air only on a 6. Count the coins in Air. 3. Put all 6 back. Now use the people's rule: a coin goes to Air on a 3, 4, 5 or 6. Count again.
flow.say: For millions of years, carbon left coal very slowly. Now people dig coal up and burn it. What happens to the Air station under the new rule?
flow.kid: Put 6 coins on Coal and Oil. Throw once for each coin. Only a 6 goes to Air. Count them. Now try again. This time 3, 4, 5 and 6 go to Air. What changed?
flow.parent: Under the first rule about 1 coin of the 6 reaches the Air. Under the people's rule about 4 do. The other tables have not changed, so carbon now arrives in the Air faster than leaves and the sea take it out.
flow.context: This is the last step of Carbon Journey. Here you change one rule to show what digging up and burning coal does to the carbon cycle.

games.title: Brown, Green or Keep Out?
games.context: This is a card game about what goes into a compost bin. Each card names one kind of waste. You say whether it is a brown, a green, or something to keep out, and why. Then you build balanced layers.

printables.title: 18 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Dry leaves swept from under a tree
items.b: Brown. Dry and tough, with much carbon and little nitrogen.
Brown. Paper is made from wood, so it is nearly all carbon-rich fibre.

items.f: A cardboard egg tray, torn up
items.b: Brown. Cardboard is thick paper. Tear it small so that decomposers can reach it.
Brown. It is dry and tough, and it keeps air spaces open in the bin.
Brown. Wood has a great deal of carbon and very little nitrogen.
Brown. The grain took most of the plant's nitrogen. The dry straw is mostly carbon.
Green. Soft and wet, with more nitrogen than dry leaves.
Green. Tea leaves are rich in nitrogen, though they look brown.
Green. Wet and soft. Decomposers eat them quickly.
Green. Fresh petals are soft and wet. Take out the thread first.
Green. Fresh grass is rich in nitrogen. A pile of only grass turns slimy and smells.

items.f: Used coffee powder from the filter
items.b: Green. The colour is brown, but used coffee powder is wet and rich in nitrogen.
Keep out. Very few decomposers have enzymes for plastic. It stays for hundreds of years.
Keep out. Glass was never alive. No decomposer eats it, and it can cut your hand.
Keep out of a small home bin. Oil coats the pieces and keeps air out, and the smell brings rats.
Keep out of a small home bin. They do rot, but they smell strongly and bring rats and flies.
Keep out. A battery holds metals that poison soil life. Give it to a battery collection point.
Keep out. They can carry germs and worms that make people ill.

rules: Shuffle the cards. Put them in a pile with the waste side up.
On your turn, take the top card. Say 'brown', 'green' or 'keep out', and give one reason.
Turn the card over. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
Play until the pile is finished. Score 1 point for every card you hold.
Now build layers. Every set of 2 browns and 1 green is one balanced layer, and scores 2 more points.
The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: the highest score possible is 24. Play again another day and try to reach it.

setup.art: A pile of cut-out cards on a table, the top card reading 'Used tea leaves'.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile, waste side up.

setup.art: A child holding a card and speaking, with a parent waiting to turn the card over.
setup.caption: 2. Say brown, green or keep out, and give a reason. Then turn the card over.

setup.art: Cards laid in sets of three on the table: two brown cards and one green card in each set.
setup.caption: 3. At the end, build layers of 2 browns and 1 green.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, waste side up. 3. Say what browns and greens are before you start.
flow.say: Browns are dry and tough, with much carbon. Greens are wet and soft, with more nitrogen. Keep out means things that would smell or bring rats, such as meat and cooked oily food.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Put them in a pile, waste side up. Browns are dry and tough. Greens are wet and soft.
flow.context: This is the first step of Brown, Green or Keep Out? Here you set up the cards and recall what browns and greens are.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to pick the top card. 2. Say brown, green or keep out, and give one reason. 3. Turn the card over. 4. Keep the card if you were right. If not, put it at the bottom.
flow.say: Is this one a brown, a green, or something to keep out? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Take the top card. Say brown, green or keep out. Give a reason. Turn the card over. Keep the card if you were right.

ask.q: Which cards were hard to decide? Why?
good: Used tea leaves and coffee powder look brown, but they are greens.
What matters is how much nitrogen and water the waste has, and the colour does not show that.

flow.parent: The names brown and green are gardeners' words. They are about carbon and nitrogen, and only roughly about colour. Tea leaves and coffee powder are the cards that catch most players.
flow.context: This is the main part of Brown, Green or Keep Out? Here you sort each kind of waste and give a reason, then check the back of the card.

flow.do: 1. Count 1 point for each card held. 2. Each player lays out sets of 2 browns and 1 green. 3. Add 2 points for each set. 4. Ask why a layer has more browns than greens.
flow.say: Build your layers. Why do you think a good bin has two parts of browns for each part of greens?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Make sets of 2 browns and 1 green. Each set scores 2 more points. Why more browns than greens?

check.q: A compost bin holds only wet vegetable peels. It smells bad. What should you add?
check.why: Dry browns soak up the extra water and keep air spaces open. They also add carbon to go with the nitrogen in the peels. More peels or more water would pack the bin tighter and keep the air out.

flow.context: This is the last step of Brown, Green or Keep Out? Here you count your points and build balanced layers of browns and greens.

experiments.title: Browns, Greens or Both: which bottle rots best?
experiments.context: In this experiment you fill three bottles with waste for decomposers to eat. One has only dry browns, one has only wet greens, and one has a mix. For 16 days you measure how far each one sinks and how it smells. You will find out which waste decomposers eat fastest without a bad smell.
experiments.question: Decomposers get the same air, the same warmth and the same spoon of soil in three bottles. Which waste will they eat fastest and without a bad smell: only browns, only greens, or a mix of both?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which bottle will sink the most in 16 days? Which bottle will smell the worst? Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All three bottles are the same size and are filled to the same height. Each gets one spoon of the same soil. All the waste is damp. The bottles stand side by side with the same cloth cover. Only the kind of waste is different.

materials.item: clear plastic bottles of 1 litre, with the tops cut off, or 3 glass jars of the same size
browns: dry leaves, torn newspaper or torn cardboard, in pieces smaller than 3 cm
greens: vegetable and fruit peels and used tea leaves, chopped smaller than 3 cm
soil from a plant pot or from under a tree
pieces of old cotton cloth and rubber bands, to cover the bottles
a ruler, a marker pen and a bowl of water

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottles and chops the peels. Keep the cloth covers on. To smell a bottle, hold it a hand's length from your face and wave the air towards your nose. Do not put your nose over it. Wash your hands with soap after every check. Anyone with asthma or an allergy to mould should leave the smell check to someone else.

schedule.what: Prepare the browns and greens. Guess. Fill the three bottles, mark the height and take the first readings.
Measure the height of each bottle. Give each a smell score. Write what you see.
Take the last readings. Work out how far each bottle sank. Explain the results. Empty the bottles safely.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 1, 5, 9, 13 and 17. Write how many centimetres each bottle sank, or draw three bars to show it. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far each bottle sank in 16 days
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different. The chart does not show smell, which matters just as much.

setup.art: Three cut plastic bottles in a row on a balcony floor: the first filled with torn paper and dry leaves, the second with chopped vegetable peels, the third with a mix, each to the same marked line.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bottles to the same height: only browns, only greens, and a mix.

setup.art: The same three bottles each covered with a square of cotton cloth held by a rubber band, with a marker line at the top of the waste.
setup.caption: 2. Add a spoon of soil to each. Mark the height. Cover with cloth.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler against the side of a bottle whose contents have sunk well below the marker line, and writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Every 4 days, measure the height and score the smell.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the tops off three 1 litre bottles, just below the shoulder. 2. Tear the browns into pieces smaller than 3 cm. 3. A grown-up chops the greens to the same size. 4. Soak the browns in a bowl of water for 2 minutes. Squeeze them out until no more water drips.
flow.say: We have two kinds of waste. Browns are dry things, like leaves and paper. Greens are wet things, like peels. Feel them both. Decomposers need damp food, so we wet the browns first.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the bottles and chop the peels. Tear the browns small. Soak the browns in water. Squeeze them out. Feel both kinds.

ask.q: How are the browns different from the greens?
good: The browns are dry, stiff and light. The greens are wet, soft and heavy.
The greens were alive a day or two ago. The browns have been dead and dry for a long time.

flow.parent: No dry leaves? Torn newspaper and cardboard alone work well. Leave out cooked food, oil, meat and fish. The browns must be damp, or the test would only show that dry things do not rot.
flow.context: This is the first step of Browns, Greens or Both. Here you prepare the two kinds of waste and notice how they differ.

flow.do: 1. Explain the three bottles: only browns, only greens, and a mix of 2 parts browns to 1 part greens. 2. Ask which will sink the most and which will smell the worst. 3. Ask for a reason each time. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Decomposers will eat what is in these bottles. Which bottle will sink the most in 16 days? Which will smell the worst? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One bottle gets browns. One gets greens. One gets a mix. Guess which will sink the most and which will smell the worst. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The greens will sink most, because they are soft and easy to eat.
The mix, because the decomposers get two kinds of food.
The greens will smell, because wet peels in our bin smell. (All fair guesses. The test will show.)

flow.parent: Do not explain carbon and nitrogen yet. Take any guess that comes with a reason, and write it down in your child's own words.
flow.context: This step of Browns, Greens or Both is for guessing. You guess which bottle will sink most and which will smell worst, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Label the bottles BROWNS, GREENS and MIX. 2. Put 3 tumblers of damp browns in the first. 3. Put 3 tumblers of greens in the second. 4. Mix 2 tumblers of browns with 1 tumbler of greens, and put them in the third. 5. Stir 1 tablespoon of soil into each. 6. Press each down gently with a flat hand, once. 7. Draw a line on each bottle at the top of the waste. Measure the height. 8. Cover each with cloth and a rubber band. 9. Stand them together in shade, out of the rain.
flow.say: The spoon of soil brings the decomposers. Why must every bottle get the same soil and stand in the same place?
flow.kid: Label three bottles. Fill one with browns. Fill one with greens. Fill one with the mix. Stir a spoon of soil into each. Press down once. Draw a line at the top. Measure the height. Cover with cloth.

ask.q: Why must every bottle get the same soil and stand in the same place?
good: So that only the kind of waste is different.
If one bottle were warmer or had more soil, we could not tell what caused the result.

flow.parent: If the three heights differ, add or take out a little waste until they match. A height of 10 to 12 cm is good. Write the day 1 heights in the table and give each bottle a smell score. Smell scores: 0 is no smell, 1 is a faint smell of earth or wet paper, 2 is sour, 3 is strong and bad.
flow.context: This step of Browns, Greens or Both sets up the test. You fill three bottles to the same height, add soil, mark the level and cover them.

flow.do: 1. Measure the height of the waste in each bottle through the side. 2. Hold each bottle a hand's length away and wave the air towards your nose. Give a smell score from 0 to 3. 3. Look for liquid, mould, darker colour and insects. 4. Write it all in the table. 5. Wash your hands with soap.
flow.say: What has changed since last time? Which bottle has sunk the most so far? Does anything surprise you?
flow.kid: Measure each bottle. Wave the air towards your nose. Give a smell score. Look for liquid, mould and colour changes. Write it down. Wash your hands.
flow.parent: What usually happens: the greens sink fast, and brown liquid collects at the bottom. They begin to smell sour or sharp within a week. The browns hardly move, though a few spots of mould may show. The mix sinks steadily and smells faintly of earth. If the browns look dry, sprinkle one spoon of water on every bottle, so the test stays fair. If the greens smell too strong to keep, write the day, and go to the challenge Rescue the Smelly Bottle.
flow.context: This step of Browns, Greens or Both is done three times, four days apart. Each time you measure how far each bottle has sunk and score the smell.

flow.do: 1. Take the last readings. 2. For each bottle, take the last height away from the first height. 3. Stand the bottles in a row, the most sunk first. Put a note by each one with the centimetres sunk and the last smell score. 4. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 5. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Take the last readings. Work out how far each bottle sank. Stand the bottles in a row, the most sunk first. Then tell your grown-up the three things.

ask.q: The browns had plenty of food in them. Why did the decomposers eat so little?
good: Dry leaves and paper are tough.
Maybe something the decomposers need is missing from browns.

ask.q: The greens sank the most. Does that make them the best compost? What does the smell tell you?
good: No. They turned wet and smelly, so something went wrong.
The smell means something is leaving the bottle into the air.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. Decomposers build their bodies from protein, so they need nitrogen as well as carbon. Paper and dry leaves hold very little nitrogen, so the decomposers multiply slowly. The fibres are also tough. This test cannot tell those two reasons apart. The greens have nitrogen, but they pack down wet, and air cannot get in. Bacteria who live without air take over and make the smell. A sharp smell is ammonia, which is nitrogen leaving for the air. The mix has both foods and air spaces.

check.q: A heap of only dry leaves rots very slowly, even when damp. What is the main thing missing?
check.why: Dry leaves are rich in carbon and poor in nitrogen. Decomposers need nitrogen to build their own bodies, so they multiply slowly on leaves alone. Choosing 'decomposers' is a fair thought, but spores and bacteria are on every leaf and in every spoon of soil. Choosing 'carbon' mixes the two up: dry leaves are mostly carbon.

flow.context: This step of Browns, Greens or Both works out the results on day 17. You find how far each bottle sank, compare the smells and explain the difference.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child would change to test their own idea. 2. Tip the mix and the browns into a plant pot or a compost bin and cover them with soil. 3. Keep the greens for the challenge Rescue the Smelly Bottle, or bury them under soil in a pot. 4. Wash the bottles and your hands.
flow.say: This test left one question open. Were the browns slow because they are tough, or because they lack nitrogen? How could we find out?
flow.kid: What would you change to test your own idea? Tip the bottles into a plant pot. Cover the waste with soil. Wash your hands.
flow.parent: One good idea is a fourth bottle of browns with two spoons of used tea leaves or coffee powder stirred in. That adds nitrogen and hardly any bulk. If it sinks faster than plain browns, nitrogen was part of the answer.
flow.context: This is the last step of Browns, Greens or Both. Here you plan a test of your own and empty the bottles safely into soil.

experiments.title: Sour Air: does carbon dioxide change water?
experiments.context: The sea takes up about a quarter of the carbon dioxide that people add to the air. In this experiment you find out what carbon dioxide does to water. You use purple cabbage water, which changes colour when water becomes more acid. You will find out whether your own breath can do that.
experiments.question: When carbon dioxide from your breath or from soda water goes into water, does the water change?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will blowing your breath through cabbage water change its colour? Will a little soda water change it? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All three glasses are the same and hold the same amount of the same cabbage water. Each glass gets 2 tablespoons of liquid added. One glass gets only plain water, so you can compare the others with it.

materials.item: leaves of purple cabbage (or 6 red hibiscus flowers)
hot drinking water, filtered if you have a filter
clear glasses of the same size
a drinking straw, a tablespoon and a tea strainer
a small bottle of plain soda water, unopened
a piece of lemon and a sheet of white paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Blow gently out through the straw and never suck. Stop and rest if you feel dizzy.

schedule.what: Make cabbage water. Guess. Blow breath into one glass and add soda water to another. Compare the colours and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three glasses. Take a photo of the three glasses side by side, or draw them in colour. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: Torn purple cabbage leaves soaking in a steel bowl of hot water that has turned deep purple-blue, with a tea strainer beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Soak torn purple cabbage in hot water for 10 minutes. Strain.

setup.art: Three clear glasses of purple-blue water standing on white paper, labelled Plain, Breath and Soda, with a child blowing through a straw into the middle one.
setup.caption: 2. Blow through a straw into one glass for 2 minutes.

setup.art: The same three glasses: the first purple-blue, the second a little more purple, the third clearly pink-purple, with a soda bottle beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Add soda water to another glass. Compare all three on white paper.

flow.do: 1. Tear 4 purple cabbage leaves into small pieces in a steel bowl. 2. A grown-up pours on 2 tumblers of hot water. 3. Wait 10 minutes, then strain and let it cool. 4. Put a spoonful on a white plate and add one drop of lemon juice. Watch the colour.
flow.say: Lemon juice is an acid. An acid is a substance that tastes sour. What did the acid do to the colour of the cabbage water?
flow.kid: Tear the cabbage leaves. Ask a grown-up to pour hot water on them. Wait 10 minutes. Strain. Add one drop of lemon to a spoonful. What happens to the colour?
flow.parent: The cabbage water should be purple or blue. Lemon turns it pink. So a move towards pink means the water has become more acid. Tap water in some towns makes the cabbage water greenish blue, which is fine. Hibiscus water starts pinkish purple and turns redder with acid.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sour Air. Here you make purple cabbage water and find out that acid turns it pink.

flow.do: 1. Stand 3 glasses on white paper. Label them PLAIN, BREATH and SODA. 2. Pour cabbage water into each, two fingers deep. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for the breath and for the soda. 4. Write the guesses and the starting colours.
flow.say: Your breath has carbon dioxide in it. So do the bubbles in soda water. Will either of them change the colour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pour cabbage water into 3 glasses, two fingers deep. Will your breath change the colour? Will soda water? Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: No change, because breath is only air. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
Soda tastes a bit sharp, so it may turn the water pink.

flow.context: This step of Sour Air is for guessing. You guess whether breath and soda water will change the colour of cabbage water, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Blow gently through the straw into the BREATH glass for 2 minutes. Rest when you need to. 2. Add 2 tablespoons of plain water to BREATH and to PLAIN. 3. Open the soda bottle. Add 2 tablespoons of soda water to SODA. 4. Hold all three against the white paper. Write the colours.
flow.say: Look at the three glasses side by side. What do you see? Which one changed the most?
flow.kid: Blow gently into BREATH for 2 minutes. Add 2 spoons of plain water to BREATH and PLAIN. Add 2 spoons of soda water to SODA. Compare the colours. Write them down.
flow.parent: The breath glass changes only a little, towards purple or pink. Look at it beside the plain glass. If you see no change, blow for 2 more minutes. The soda glass changes clearly. The plain water is added so that every glass is thinned by the same amount.
flow.context: This is the main step of Sour Air. Here you blow breath into one glass, add soda water to another and compare the colours.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 2. Then stir the SODA glass hard with a spoon for 2 minutes. 3. Compare its colour again.
flow.say: Tell me what you thought, what you saw and why. Now stir the soda glass hard. What happens to the colour, and what do you think has left the water?
flow.kid: Tell your grown-up what you thought, what you saw and why. Now stir the SODA glass hard for 2 minutes. Does the colour change back?

ask.q: What does the colour change tell you about carbon dioxide and water?
good: Carbon dioxide goes into water and makes the water a little acid.
When the gas leaves, the water goes back towards the first colour.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. Carbon dioxide dissolves in water and joins with it to make a weak acid. Stirring drives the gas out, so the colour moves part of the way back. Carbon moves between air and water in both directions.
flow.context: This step of Sour Air explains the results. You say what the colours show, then stir the gas out of the soda glass and watch the colour move back.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that the sea takes up about a quarter of the carbon dioxide people add to the air. 2. Ask what that might do to sea water. 3. Ask who in the sea might be affected.
flow.say: The sea has been taking up carbon dioxide from the air for 200 years. What do you think is happening to the sea water? Who lives in it and builds shells?
flow.kid: Think about your soda glass. Then tell your grown-up who in the sea builds shells. What might happen to them?
flow.parent: Sea water is not sour. It is slightly alkaline, which is the opposite of acid, and it is slowly becoming less so. In water that is more acid, corals, snails and some tiny algae must work harder to build shells. How much harm this will do is still being measured.

check.q: The sea takes up carbon dioxide from the air. What happens to the sea water?
options: It slowly becomes a little more acid
check.why: Carbon dioxide joins with water to make a weak acid, as it did in your glass. The sea is still slightly alkaline, but less than before. Salt has nothing to do with this gas. 'Nothing changes' forgets that the gas does not vanish in water. It reacts with the water.

flow.context: This is the last step of Sour Air. Here you link what happened in the glass to what happens when the sea takes up carbon dioxide.

activities.title: Two Heaps: sort one day's waste
activities.context: This short activity starts the unit. You sort one day's waste from your home into two heaps and compare them with your hands, eyes and nose. You will find out how different the two heaps feel and smell. You do not explain anything yet. You only notice and wonder.

materials.item: one day's vegetable and fruit peels, used tea leaves and old flowers
dry things that were once alive: fallen leaves, newspaper, a cardboard box, coconut fibre
an old newspaper to work on

activities.record: Take a photo of the two heaps, or draw them. Write three things you noticed about each, and one question you want answered.

setup.art: An open newspaper on a kitchen floor with a mixed pile of peels, tea leaves, dry leaves, torn cardboard and a plastic wrapper.
setup.caption: 1. Tip one day's waste onto a newspaper.

setup.art: The same newspaper with two heaps: wet soft peels on the left, dry leaves and paper on the right, and a plastic wrapper set aside.
setup.caption: 2. Make two heaps: wet and soft, dry and tough. Compare them.

flow.do: 1. Tip the waste onto the newspaper. 2. Put aside anything that was never alive, such as plastic, foil and glass. 3. Sort the rest into two heaps: wet and soft, or dry and tough.
flow.say: Everything left on the paper was once part of a living being. Let's make two heaps. Which things are wet and soft? Which are dry and tough?
flow.kid: Tip the waste onto the newspaper. Take out plastic, foil and glass. Make two heaps. One is wet and soft. One is dry and tough.
flow.parent: Used tea leaves go with the wet heap. Paper and cardboard go with the dry heap, because they are made from wood.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Heaps. Here you sort one day's waste into a wet, soft heap and a dry, tough heap.

flow.do: 1. Lift a handful from each heap and compare the weight. 2. Squeeze each handful. 3. Tear a piece from each. 4. Smell each from a hand's length away. 5. Ask what your child notices.
flow.say: Hold some of each. Squeeze, tear and smell. What do you notice? Tell me everything, even small things.
flow.kid: Lift some of each heap. Which is heavier? Squeeze each. Tear a piece of each. Smell each from a distance.

ask.q: What do you notice?
good: The wet heap is heavier and water comes out when I squeeze.
