The dry heap is stiff and hard to tear, and it has almost no smell.
The wet heap already smells a little.

flow.context: This step of Two Heaps compares the heaps. You lift, squeeze, tear and smell a handful of each, and say what you notice.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child wonders about the two heaps. 2. Ask which heap decomposers would finish first, and why. 3. Write down one question to keep. Do not answer it yet.
flow.say: What do you wonder? Decomposers are the tiny living beings, such as bacteria and fungi, that eat dead plants and animals. If they came to eat these heaps, which would they finish first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What do you wonder about the heaps? Which heap would decomposers finish first? Why? Write down one question.

ask.q: The peel was part of a vegetable. Where was the stuff of the vegetable before that?
good: In the soil and the water.
In the air. (Rare, and right for most of it. Do not say so yet.)

flow.parent: Keep both heaps. They are the browns and the greens for the experiment Browns, Greens or Both.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Heaps. Here you say what you wonder, and guess which heap decomposers would finish first.

activities.title: Protein Hunt: find the nitrogen in your kitchen
activities.context: Every protein has nitrogen in it. In this activity you read the labels on food packets to find out which foods in your kitchen hold the most protein, and so the most nitrogen.

materials.item: food packets with a nutrition label, such as dal, rice, atta, groundnuts, milk, biscuits, sugar and oil
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with two columns: the food, and the grams of protein in 100 grams. Write the foods in order, from the most protein to the least.

setup.art: Six food packets lined up on a kitchen counter: toor dal, rice, groundnuts, a milk packet, biscuits and sugar, each turned to show the nutrition label.
setup.caption: 1. Find 6 packets with a nutrition label.

setup.art: A close view of a nutrition label with a child's finger on the line that says 'Protein', and a notebook table beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Read the protein in 100 grams. Write the foods in order.

flow.do: 1. Collect 6 food packets that have a nutrition label. 2. Find the line that says 'Protein'. 3. Check that the number is for 100 grams, or 100 millilitres for milk.
flow.say: Protein is what muscles, hair and enzymes are built from. Every protein has nitrogen in it. Which of these foods do you think has the most protein? Why?
flow.kid: Collect 6 food packets. Find the word 'Protein' on each label. Which food do you think has the most? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Protein Hunt. Here you find the protein line on the labels of six foods and guess which has the most.

flow.do: 1. Write each food and the grams of protein in 100 grams. 2. Put the foods in order, from most to least. 3. Circle any food that has none.
flow.say: Read out each number. Which food comes first? Which foods have no protein at all?
flow.kid: Write each food and the protein number. Put the foods in order. Circle any food with zero protein.
flow.parent: Usual numbers for 100 grams: groundnuts about 25 grams, toor dal and urad dal about 22, atta about 11, rice about 7, milk about 3. Sugar and oil have none. Sugar and oil are built of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.
flow.context: This step of Protein Hunt reads the labels. You write the protein in 100 grams of each food and put the foods in order.

flow.do: 1. Ask which family of plants the top foods come from. 2. Ask where a dal plant could get so much nitrogen. 3. Tell your child that about 16 of every 100 grams of protein is nitrogen.
flow.say: Dal and groundnuts are near the top. They are seeds of the bean family. Where do you think these plants get so much nitrogen?
flow.kid: Which foods came top? What plant family are they from?

ask.q: Where could a dal plant get so much nitrogen?
good: From bacteria in the roots, who take nitrogen from the air.
From the soil, or from fertiliser. (Partly true for every plant.)

check.q: Which of these foods holds the most nitrogen in 100 grams?
check.why: Nitrogen is in protein, and toor dal has about three times as much protein as rice. Sugar has no protein and no nitrogen at all. Choosing rice is natural, because we eat so much of it. But the label shows it holds less protein in each 100 grams.

flow.context: This is the last step of Protein Hunt. Here you ask why the seeds of the bean family hold so much protein and nitrogen.

activities.title: Draw the Loop: one carbon atom from the air to your idli and back
activities.context: A model is something you make to show what you cannot see. In this activity you make a model of the path of one carbon atom, from the air, through a paddy plant and an idli, through you, and back to the air. You will find out that the same carbon goes round and round.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper
a pencil and two colour pencils

activities.record: Keep your loop, or take a photo of it. Each arrow should have the name of what happens written beside it.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with five small drawings in a ring: a cloud of air, a paddy plant, a plate of idli, a child, and the child's breath.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the places one carbon atom visits, in a ring.

setup.art: The same sheet with arrows joining the drawings, each arrow labelled with a word such as 'photosynthesis' or 'respiration', and a gas stove drawn to one side with a single arrow.
setup.caption: 2. Join them with arrows. Name what happens at each arrow.

flow.do: 1. Ask what an idli is made of. 2. Write five places on five slips of paper: the air, a paddy plant, an idli, you, and your breath. Lay them in a ring on the big sheet. 3. Put one black dot, the carbon atom, on the air slip.
flow.say: An idli is rice and ulundu. Both are seeds. Let's follow one carbon atom. Where was it before it was in the rice? How did it get in?
flow.kid: What is an idli made of? Make five slips: air, paddy plant, idli, you, and your breath. Lay them in a ring. Put one black dot on the air slip.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Loop. Here you draw the five places that one carbon atom passes through on the way to you and back.

flow.do: 1. Draw an arrow from each place to the next. 2. Beside each arrow, write what happens there. 3. Ask how long the whole round might take.
flow.say: What happens at each arrow? Use the real words: photosynthesis, eating, respiration. How long do you think one round takes?
flow.kid: Draw an arrow from each place to the next. Write what happens beside each arrow. How long does one round take?
flow.parent: Air to leaf is photosynthesis. Leaf to grain is the plant storing starch. Grain to you is eating and digesting. You to your breath is respiration. One round takes a few months to a year, most of it spent as stored rice.
flow.context: This step of Draw the Loop adds the arrows. You name what happens to the carbon atom at each arrow.

flow.do: 1. Write GAS STOVE on a slip and lay it outside the ring. 2. Ask where the carbon in cooking gas came from. 3. Lay a spoon from the stove slip to the air slip, as its arrow. 4. Ask how this arrow is different from the others.
flow.say: The stove burns gas from deep under the ground. Lay a spoon from the stove slip to the air slip, as that carbon's arrow. How is this arrow different from all the others?
flow.kid: Write GAS STOVE on a slip. Its carbon came from deep underground. Lay a spoon from the stove slip to the air slip, as its arrow.

ask.q: How is the stove's arrow different from the others?
good: It goes one way. Nothing takes that carbon back underground.
The other arrows make a ring, so the air gets back what it gave.

flow.context: This is the last step of Draw the Loop. Here you add the carbon from cooking gas and see that its arrow goes one way only.

activities.title: The Nitrogen Relay: pass one atom all the way round
activities.context: This is an act-out of the nitrogen cycle. A ball marked N is a nitrogen atom. It passes through six pairs of hands, and each one says what they do to it. You can also play it alone with six paper cups.

materials.item: a small ball, a lemon or a marble, to be the nitrogen atom
slips of paper for the six labels
paper cups or steel tumblers, if you play alone

activities.record: Keep your ring of six labels. Write beside each one what happens to the nitrogen atom there.

setup.art: Six paper labels laid in a ring on the floor: Air, Fixing Bacteria, Plant, Animal, Decomposer, Air-Returning Bacteria.
setup.caption: 1. Lay six labels in a ring.

setup.art: A family of three standing at the labels and passing a lemon marked N from hand to hand round the ring.
setup.caption: 2. Pass the atom round. Each station says what they do.

flow.do: 1. Write six labels: AIR, FIXING BACTERIA, PLANT, ANIMAL, DECOMPOSER, AIR-RETURNING BACTERIA. 2. Lay them in a ring in that order. 3. Stand a person or a cup at each. 4. Mark the ball with an N.
flow.say: This ball is one nitrogen atom. In the air it is stuck to a partner. Who in this ring can pull it free? Who do you think comes next?
flow.kid: Write the six labels. Lay them in a ring. Put a cup at each one. The ball is one nitrogen atom. Who can take it from the air?
flow.parent: With fewer than six people, each person takes two stations next to each other.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Nitrogen Relay. Here you lay out the six stations of the nitrogen cycle in a ring.

flow.do: 1. Start the ball at AIR and pass it round. 2. Each station says their line as they take the ball. 3. Go round three times, a little faster each time.
flow.say: Say your line as you take the atom. Air: 'I hold nitrogen in pairs.' Fixing bacteria: 'I split the pair and make ammonia.' Plant: 'I build protein.' Animal: 'I eat the plant.' Decomposer: 'I rot what dies.' Air-returning bacteria: 'I turn it back into gas in the air.'
flow.kid: Pass the ball round the ring. Say each station's line. Fixing bacteria split the pair. The plant builds protein. The animal eats the plant.
flow.parent: The other lines. Animal: 'I eat the plant and pass nitrogen out in urine.' Decomposer: 'I free the nitrogen from dung and dead bodies.' Air-returning bacteria: 'I send nitrogen gas back to the air.' Between the decomposer and the plant there is a short cut. Soil bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate, and roots take it up again without it ever reaching the air.
flow.context: This is the main step of The Nitrogen Relay. Here you pass one nitrogen atom round the ring, and each station says what they do to it.

flow.do: 1. Take away the FIXING BACTERIA station and try to pass the ball. 2. Put it back. Take away the DECOMPOSER and try again. 3. Add a new station called FACTORY beside the fixing bacteria. Ask what it changes.
flow.say: What happens to the ring when the fixing bacteria are gone? What about when the decomposers are gone? Where does the atom get stuck each time?
flow.kid: Take away the fixing bacteria. Can the ball get round? Put them back. Take away the decomposer. Try to pass the ball round again.

ask.q: Where does the nitrogen get stuck without decomposers?
good: In dung and dead bodies. The plants cannot get it back.
The plants would run short, even though the nitrogen is lying right there.

check.q: Who takes nitrogen from the air and makes it usable for a bean plant?
check.why: Only certain bacteria have the enzyme that splits a pair of nitrogen atoms. Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air, and it is easy to think they take nitrogen as well. They do not. Earthworms help to break up dead matter, and they do not fix nitrogen.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Nitrogen Relay. Here you take one station away at a time and see where the nitrogen atom gets stuck.

activities.title: Read the Keeling Curve: 65 years of air on one page
activities.context: Since 1958, scientists on a mountain in Hawaii have measured how much carbon dioxide is in the air. In this activity you plot their real numbers as a line graph and read what the line shows.

materials.item: a sheet of graph paper, or a page of a squared maths notebook
a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Keep your graph. Under it, write how much the number rose in each ten years.

setup.art: A sheet of graph paper with years from 1960 to 2030 along the bottom and numbers from 300 to 440 up the side, and a child marking a dot.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the years along the bottom and the numbers up the side.

setup.art: The same graph with eight dots joined by a line that climbs more steeply towards the right.
setup.caption: 2. Plot the 8 points and join them. Look at how the line bends.

flow.do: 1. Draw the bottom line with the years 1960 to 2030, one square for every 5 years. 2. Draw the side line from 300 to 440, one square for every 10. 3. Plot these 8 points. 1960: 317. 1970: 326. 1980: 339. 1990: 354. 2000: 370. 2010: 390. 2020: 414. 2025: 427.
flow.say: Each number says how many particles of carbon dioxide were in a million particles of air that year. Before you join the dots, what shape do you expect?
flow.kid: Draw the years along the bottom. Draw 300 to 440 up the side. Plot the 8 points. What shape will the line make? Guess first.
flow.parent: These are the yearly averages measured at Mauna Loa in Hawaii, rounded to whole numbers. They are published by the United States weather and ocean agency, NOAA.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Keeling Curve. Here you plot eight real measurements of the carbon dioxide in the air, from 1960 to 2025.

flow.do: 1. Join the points. 2. Work out the rise in each ten years: 1960 to 1970, 1970 to 1980, and so on up to 2020. 3. Write the six rises in a row. 4. Ask what the pattern is.
flow.say: How much did the number rise in each ten years? Is the line straight, or does it bend? What does the bend mean?
flow.kid: Join the points. Work out the rise in each ten years. Write the six rises in a row. Is the line straight or bent?

ask.q: What does the bend in the line mean?
good: The number is rising faster now than it did before.
People are burning more coal, oil and gas each year than they used to.

flow.parent: The six rises are 9, 13, 15, 16, 20 and 24. Each is bigger than the one before, so the line bends upwards.
flow.context: This step of Read the Keeling Curve reads the line. You work out the rise in each ten years and see that the rise is speeding up.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to carry the line on by eye to 2035 and read the number. 2. Tell them that the real line also wobbles up and down a little each year. 3. Ask what could take carbon dioxide out of the air every summer.
flow.say: The real line dips a little every northern summer and rises every winter. What takes carbon dioxide out of the air in summer?
flow.kid: Carry your line on to 2035. What number do you read? The real line dips every summer. Tell your grown-up your idea about why.
flow.parent: Most of the world's land and forests are in the northern half. In the northern summer those forests are in leaf and take in more carbon dioxide than living beings give out. In winter many leaves fall and rot, and the number rises again. A fair reading for 2035 is 450 to 455, if nothing changes.

check.q: The carbon dioxide in the air dips a little every northern summer. Why?
options: Forests in leaf take in more carbon
check.why: In summer the great northern forests photosynthesise and take in more carbon dioxide than living beings breathe out. Factories do not close for the summer. Warm air holding less gas is true of water, not of the open air.

flow.context: This is the last step of Read the Keeling Curve. Here you carry the line forward, and learn why the real line dips every summer.

activities.title: Root Dig: look for nodules (if you have a garden, a park or a farm nearby)
activities.context: Plants of the bean family keep nitrogen-fixing bacteria in small lumps on their roots, called nodules. In this activity you dig up one such plant and one other plant, wash the roots and compare them.

materials.item: a plant of the bean family that you are allowed to dig up, such as beans, groundnut, cowpea or touch-me-not
a tuft of grass or another weed, to compare
a trowel or an old spoon, and a bucket of water

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along and chooses where to dig. Ask before you dig up any plant that someone is growing. Wash your hands with soap afterwards.
activities.record: Take a photo of both sets of roots, or draw them. Write how many nodules you counted, and the colour inside one.

setup.art: A child with an old spoon digging a wide circle round a small bean plant in a garden bed, lifting the plant with a ball of soil.
setup.caption: 1. Dig a wide circle round the plant. Lift the plant with the soil on.

setup.art: Two root systems held up after washing in a bucket: bean roots with small round nodules and grass roots with none.
setup.caption: 2. Wash the roots gently. Look for small round lumps.

flow.do: 1. Find a plant of the bean family at least a month old. 2. Dig a circle about 10 cm from the stem and a spoon deep. 3. Lift the plant with the soil still on. Do not pull the stem, or the nodules will break off. 4. Dig up a tuft of grass the same way.
flow.say: We will look at the roots of two plants. One is from the bean family. Do you think their roots will look the same? Why?
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up. Dig a wide circle round the bean plant. Lift the plant with the soil on. Do not pull the stem. Dig up some grass too.
flow.parent: Touch-me-not, which grows wild on roadsides and in empty plots, is of the bean family and usually has nodules. If you have only pots, sow five cowpea or bean seeds in soil from a garden and dig one up after five weeks.
flow.context: This is the first step of Root Dig. Here you dig up a plant of the bean family and a tuft of grass without breaking their roots.

flow.do: 1. Swish each root gently in the bucket until the soil falls away. 2. Look for round lumps on the bean roots. 3. Count them. 4. Look for any on the grass roots.
flow.say: What do you see on the bean roots? Are they on the grass roots too? What do you wonder about them?
flow.kid: Swish the roots in water. Look for small round lumps. Count them. Does the grass have any?
flow.parent: Nodules are 1 to 5 mm across and sit on the side of a root. They come off easily when rubbed. If you find none, the right bacteria may be missing from that soil, or the soil may be rich in nitrogen. Both are worth writing down.
flow.context: This step of Root Dig washes the roots. You look for nodules on the bean plant and check whether the grass has any.

flow.do: 1. Pick off the biggest nodule and split it with a fingernail. 2. Look at the colour inside. 3. Lay both roots side by side on white paper. Take a photo, or draw them. 4. Plant the grass back.
flow.say: Split one open. What colour is it inside? Pink or red means the bacteria inside are fixing nitrogen.
flow.kid: Split the biggest lump with your fingernail. What colour is it inside? Lay both roots side by side. Take a photo, or draw them.

ask.q: Why does the grass have no nodules, and how does grass get nitrogen?
good: Grass does not keep these bacteria. Grass takes up nitrogen that is already in the soil.
Some of that soil nitrogen came from dead bean roots and from decomposers.

flow.parent: A nodule that is white, green or brown inside is not fixing nitrogen now. It may be too young or too old.
flow.context: This is the last step of Root Dig. Here you split a nodule to see its colour and draw the two sets of roots.

projects.title: Bottle World: a sealed jar for four weeks
projects.context: In this four-week project you plant a small plant in a glass jar and close the lid tightly. Nothing goes in after that except light. You will find out whether a plant can live for four weeks with nothing added. You watch what happens, and show how water and carbon go round inside.

materials.item: a clear glass jar with a tight lid, about 1 litre
small pebbles
soil from a plant pot or a garden
a small plant with roots: a rooted money plant cutting, a small fern, or moss from a damp wall
dry leaves, and water

schedule.what: Build the jar, guess what will happen, and close the lid.
Look for water drops, new growth and changes in the dry leaf. Draw the jar.
Make the last drawing. Add the water loop and the carbon loop to it.

projects.record: Take a photo or make a drawing of the jar each week. On the last drawing, add arrows to show how water goes round and how carbon goes round inside the jar, or tell it to a grown-up.

setup.art: A glass jar with a layer of pebbles at the bottom, dark soil above, a small money plant cutting planted in the soil and one dry leaf lying on top.
setup.caption: 1. Pebbles, then soil, then a small plant and a dry leaf.

setup.art: The same jar with the lid screwed on, standing on a shelf near a bright window but out of the direct sun, with drops of water on the inside of the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Add 3 spoons of water. Close the lid. Keep the jar in bright shade.

flow.do: 1. Put 2 cm of pebbles in the jar, then 4 cm of soil. 2. Plant the small plant. Lay a dry leaf on the soil. 3. Add 3 tablespoons of water. The soil should be damp, with no water standing in the pebbles. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason. 5. Close the lid tightly and write the date on it. 6. Stand the jar in a bright place that gets no direct sun.
flow.say: Once the lid is on, no air and no water can get in or out. What do you think will happen to the plant in four weeks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put pebbles in the jar. Add soil. Plant the small plant. Lay a dry leaf on top. Add 3 spoons of water. What will happen with the lid shut? Close the lid.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The plant will die, because the air will run out. (A common guess. Wait and see.)
The plant will be fine, because plants make their own oxygen.
The plant will dry up, because nobody will water them.

flow.parent: Direct sun heats a closed jar like a parked car and cooks the plant. A shelf near a window is right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bottle World. Here you build a small garden in a jar, guess what will happen and close the lid.

flow.wait: Look once a week, on days 8, 15 and 22
flow.do: 1. Without opening the jar, look for drops on the glass. 2. Look for new leaves or roots. 3. Look at the dry leaf. 4. Look for mould. 5. Take a photo of the jar, or draw it.
flow.say: What has changed since last week? Where did the drops on the glass come from? Where do they go?
flow.kid: Do not open the jar. Look for water drops. Look for new leaves. Look at the dry leaf. Take a photo of the jar, or draw it.
flow.parent: Drops on the glass in the morning that clear by afternoon are a good sign. If the glass is fogged all day, open the lid for one day and close it again. Write that down. A little white mould on the dry leaf is the decomposers at work. If the plant rots, start again with less water.
flow.context: This step of Bottle World is done once a week for three weeks. You look into the sealed jar and draw what has changed.

flow.do: 1. Take the last photo or drawing. 2. Ask where the water in the jar goes each day. Trace that loop with a finger on the glass. 3. Ask where the plant gets carbon dioxide, and who makes it. Trace that loop too. 4. Ask what comes into the jar and what leaves.
flow.say: The plant has had no new air for four weeks. Where does the carbon dioxide for the leaves come from? Who in the jar is making it?
flow.kid: Take your last photo or drawing. Trace with a finger how the water goes round the jar. Then trace how the carbon goes round.

ask.q: Who in the jar makes carbon dioxide, and who uses it?
good: The decomposers in the soil make it when they eat the dry leaf. The plant also respires.
The plant's leaves use it in the light to build sugar.

ask.q: What comes into the jar from outside, and what leaves?
good: Only light comes in. Only heat leaves.
The atoms stay inside and go round. The Earth is like this too.

flow.parent: A sealed jar is a small model of the Earth. Matter stays in and goes round, and energy passes through. Newspapers have reported a man in England, David Latimer, whose sealed bottle garden has not been watered since 1972.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bottle World. Here you draw how water and carbon go round inside the sealed jar, and what crosses the glass.

challenges.title: Rescue the Smelly Bottle
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the experiment Browns, Greens or Both, the bottle of only greens turned wet, sunken and smelly. Here you change that bottle so that the decomposers who need air can work again and the smell fades.
challenges.problem: Change the smelly bottle of greens so that, 5 days later, its smell score is 1 or less. You may not throw any of the greens away.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
All the greens must stay in the bottle or a bigger pot.
You may not hide the smell with scent, agarbatti or a tight lid.
Flies must still be kept out.
materials: the bottle of greens from the experiment, or one day's wet waste kept in a closed box for 3 days
dry leaves, torn newspaper, cardboard or coconut fibre
a stick or an old spoon
a cloth and a rubber band
a nail, for a grown-up to make air holes
general: Mix in two parts of dry browns for each part of greens.
Make air holes in the sides and the bottom of the bottle.
Drain the liquid into a plant pot that has plenty of soil.
creative: Stand a rolled tube of cardboard in the middle, as a chimney for air.
Put a layer of coconut fibre at the bottom to hold the waste up out of the liquid.
Stir the bottle with a stick every day, to let air in.
Add a spoon of finished compost or soil, to bring more decomposers.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own rescue. Write what you think went wrong, and what each change is meant to fix. Score the smell before you start and again after 5 days.

setup.art: A cut plastic bottle half full of dark, wet, sunken vegetable waste with liquid at the bottom, and a child holding their nose at arm's length.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the smelly bottle. What went wrong?

setup.art: The same bottle now with torn paper and dry leaves mixed in, air holes in the sides, a cardboard tube standing in the middle and a cloth cover.
setup.caption: 2. Add browns and air. Score the smell again after 5 days.

flow.do: 1. Look at the bottle through the side. 2. Score the smell from a hand's length away, from 0 (no smell) to 3 (very bad). 3. Ask what the decomposers in this bottle are short of. 4. Write a plan with at least two changes.
flow.say: This bottle has plenty of food. So what are the decomposers short of? What will you change, and what will each change fix?
flow.kid: Look at the bottle. Score the smell. Then plan two changes. Say what each one fixes.

ask.q: What are the decomposers in this bottle short of?
good: Air, because the wet greens have packed down.
Carbon-rich browns to go with all the nitrogen.

flow.context: This is the first step of Rescue the Smelly Bottle. Here you work out what went wrong in the bottle of greens and plan how to fix it.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes any air holes with a heated nail held in pliers. 2. Tip the greens into a bowl, outdoors or on a balcony. 3. Carry out your plan. 4. Put everything back and cover it with cloth. 5. Wash your hands with soap.
flow.say: Carry out your plan. As you mix, look closely. Is the waste at the bottom different from the waste at the top?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make the air holes. Tip the greens into a bowl outdoors. Carry out your plan. Cover the bottle with cloth. Wash your hands.
flow.parent: The waste at the bottom is usually darker, wetter and smellier, because the least air reached it. If the mix will not fit in the bottle, use a flowerpot with a hole in the base.
flow.context: This step of Rescue the Smelly Bottle carries out your plan. You add browns and air to the bottle of greens.

flow.do: 1. Score the smell again. 2. Compare it with the first score. 3. Ask which change did the most, and how you could test that. 4. Tip the waste into a plant pot and cover it with soil.
flow.say: What is the smell score now? Which of your changes do you think did the most? How could we find out for certain?
flow.kid: Score the smell again. Is it lower? Which change did the most? How could you test that?

check.q: A compost bin smells rotten and is very wet. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too much air is getting in
Too little air is getting in
Too many dry leaves were added
check.why: When wet waste packs down, air cannot reach the middle. Bacteria who live without air take over, and they give off bad-smelling gases. Too many dry leaves would make the bin slow, not smelly. More air cures the smell.

flow.context: This is the last step of Rescue the Smelly Bottle. Here you score the smell again after 5 days and decide which change helped most.

challenges.title: Keep It in the Field: stop the rain from washing fertiliser away
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Nitrate fertiliser dissolves in water, so rain can wash it off a field into streams and lakes. Here you build a small sloping field, use food colour as pretend fertiliser, and design a field that loses less.
challenges.problem: Design a small sloping field that loses as little colour as possible when one tumbler of rain falls on it.
constraints: Use the same amount of soil, the same slope, the same rain and the same 5 drops of colour as the bare field.
The colour must go on or in the soil of the field. It may not be left out.
Use only things you have at home.
materials: 2 steel plates with a rim, or 2 shallow trays
food colour or ink, and a dropper or a spoon
a paper cup with 5 small holes in the base, to make rain
2 clear glasses, 2 big bowls or basins, a book 3 cm thick and white paper
dry leaves, straw, small sticks, cloth and clay or wet atta
general: Cover the soil with dry leaves or straw, as farmers do with mulch.
Build small ridges of soil across the slope, like the bunds of a paddy field.
Press small plants or grass with roots into the soil.
creative: Put the colour in a hole 2 cm deep and cover it, in place of dropping it on top.
Give the colour in two halves, with a little rain between.
Wrap the colour in a small ball of clay or wet atta, so that it comes out slowly.
Dig a small pit at the bottom of the slope to catch the water.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own field. Plan it first, by drawing it or telling it, and say why each part is there. Test it against the bare field with the same rain. Then change one thing and test again.

setup.art: A steel plate filled with pressed soil, propped on a book so that it slopes, with its lower edge resting inside a large bowl and drops of red colour on the soil.
setup.caption: 1. Make a sloping field of soil. Drop 5 drops of colour on top.

setup.art: A child holding a paper cup with holes above the sloping plate as water sprinkles down, and red-tinted water running into the bowl below.
setup.caption: 2. Sprinkle one tumbler of rain. Catch what runs off.

setup.art: Two clear glasses on white paper, one holding dark red water and one holding pale pink water, labelled Bare Field and My Field.
setup.caption: 3. Pour the run-off into clear glasses. Paler means less was lost.

flow.do: 1. Work in a bathroom or on a balcony. 2. Press 2 tumblers of soil flat on a plate. 3. Prop one side on the book. Rest the lower edge inside a big bowl. 4. Drop 5 drops of colour on the upper half. 5. Sprinkle 1 tumbler of water from the cup with holes, held a hand's length above. 6. Pour the run-off into a clear glass.
flow.say: This is the bare field. The colour is our pretend fertiliser. Watch where it goes when the rain comes. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Press soil flat on a plate. Prop one side on a book. Drop 5 drops of colour on top. Sprinkle one tumbler of rain. Catch the run-off in a glass.
flow.parent: Food colour dissolves and moves with water, much as nitrate does. Keep this glass. It is what the new design must beat.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep It in the Field. Here you build a bare sloping field and see how much pretend fertiliser the rain carries off.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to plan a design, by drawing it or by telling it, and give a reason for each part. 2. Build it on the second plate with 2 tumblers of soil. 3. Use the same slope and put on the same 5 drops.
flow.say: How will you keep the colour in your field? Why do you think that will work?
flow.kid: Plan your design. Draw it or tell it to your grown-up. Say why each part is there. Build it on the second plate. Use the same slope. Add the same 5 drops.
flow.context: This step of Keep It in the Field is for designing. You draw and build a field that you think will lose less colour in the rain.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle 1 tumbler of rain in the same way as before. 2. Pour the run-off into the second clear glass. 3. Stand both glasses on white paper and compare. 4. Compare how much water ran off as well.
flow.say: Which glass is paler? Which holds less water? What does that tell you about your design?
flow.kid: Sprinkle the same rain. Catch the run-off in the second glass. Put both glasses on white paper. Which is paler? Which has less water?

ask.q: Your field lost less colour. Where is the colour now, and is that good for a real crop?
good: It is still in the soil, where roots could take it up.
Some may have sunk straight down below the roots, which is also a loss.

flow.context: This step of Keep It in the Field tests your design. You give it the same rain as the bare field and compare the two glasses of run-off.

flow.do: 1. Ask which one change your child would make next. 2. Link the designs to real farms: mulch, bunds, small doses and coated urea. 3. Pour the soil into a plant pot.
flow.say: Real farmers use the same ideas. A bund is a low wall of soil that holds water back. Which of your ideas is like a bund? Which is like giving fertiliser in small amounts?
flow.kid: What one thing would you change next? Which of your ideas do real farmers use? Pour the soil into a plant pot.

check.q: Why does rain wash nitrate fertiliser out of a bare field so easily?
check.why: Nitrate dissolves in water and does not stick to soil grains, so it goes wherever the water goes. It does not float, and its weight is not the reason. That is why slowing the water and giving small doses both help.

flow.context: This is the last step of Keep It in the Field. Here you choose your next change and link your design to what real farmers do.

items.p: Where does most of the dry weight of a tree come from?
items.why: A leaf takes carbon dioxide from the air and builds sugar, and the tree builds wood from sugar. Soil gives water and minerals, which are a small part of the weight. Sunlight gives energy, and energy has no weight to add.

items.p: True or false: when a log rots, the atoms of the log are destroyed.
items.why: False. Decomposers take the log apart. The atoms move into the air, the soil and the decomposers' own bodies. No atom is destroyed.

items.p: Green plants take carbon out of the air by ____.
items.why: In photosynthesis a plant uses light to join carbon dioxide and water into sugar.

items.p: Does each of these take carbon out of the air, or put carbon into the air? Sort them.
items.why: Only photosynthesis takes carbon out of the air. Respiration, rotting and burning all put carbon into the air as carbon dioxide.
cats: Takes carbon out of the air
items: Takes carbon out of the air
Takes carbon out of the air
Takes carbon out of the air

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These five words are needed to talk about any matter cycle. A strong answer could give an example of each from a paddy field.
pairs: a place where atoms stay for a time
the movement of atoms from one store to another
changing nitrogen gas into a form plants can use
getting energy from food and giving off carbon dioxide
a plant of the bean family

items.p: Put the path of one nitrogen atom in order, starting from the air.
items.why: Bacteria fix the nitrogen, and the plant builds it into protein. You eat the protein and build your own. Spare nitrogen leaves your body in urine.

items.p: In Browns, Greens or Both, the bottle of only browns hardly sank. Explain why, using the word 'nitrogen'.
items.a: Dry leaves and paper have a lot of carbon and very little nitrogen. Decomposers need nitrogen to build their bodies. With so little nitrogen they could not multiply fast, so they ate the browns very slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says that decomposers are living beings who need nitrogen as well as carbon. It may add that browns are also tough.

items.p: Draw the carbon cycle with four places: the air, a plant, an animal and the soil. Label each arrow.
items.a: Arrows go from air to plant (photosynthesis), plant to animal (eating), plant and animal to soil (dead leaves, dung, bodies), and from plant, animal and soil back to air (respiration).
items.why: A strong drawing has only one arrow out of the air and at least three arrows back into it. Each arrow carries the name of what happens.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Three of these plants are legumes. Which one is not?
items.why: Rice is a grass. Groundnut, black gram and beans are of the bean family, and keep nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules.

items.p: Why can a paddy plant not use the nitrogen in the air?
opts: The air has too little nitrogen
Nitrogen atoms are held in tight pairs
items.why: The air is mostly nitrogen, so there is plenty. But each nitrogen atom is joined very strongly to a partner, and a plant has no enzyme to split them.

items.p: True or false: about 78 of every 100 particles of air are nitrogen.
items.why: True. Most of the air is nitrogen gas. Oxygen is about 21 of every 100, and carbon dioxide is far less than 1.

items.p: A root nodule that is fixing nitrogen is ____ inside.
items.why: The colour comes from a red protein that carries oxygen to the bacteria in small amounts. A white or green nodule is not working.

items.p: Label each store of carbon 'fast' or 'slow': a leaf, limestone, a cow, coal.
items.why: Carbon passes through leaves and animals within months or years. Carbon in rock and coal stays for millions of years.
items.art: Four small drawings in a row, a leaf, a block of limestone, a cow and a lump of coal, each with a blank box below.

items.p: A compost bin on a balcony smells bad. Two neighbours give different advice.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the second neighbour and uses the test: the bottle of only greens smelled, and the mix did not. It also grants that the first neighbour is right about one thing. A badly kept bin does smell, and neighbours should not have to put up with it.
items.why: The smell is real, and so is the cure. A bin smells when it is too wet and has too little air, and browns fix both.

views.says: Throw it out. Compost always smells. Kitchen waste belongs in the dustbin lorry.
Add dry leaves and stir it. A bin smells only when it is too wet and has no air.

items.ask: Which neighbour do you agree with? Use what you saw in your compost test. Then say one thing the other neighbour has right.

items.p: Used tea leaves look brown. Why do they count as a 'green' in compost?
opts: They are wet and rich in nitrogen
items.why: The words brown and green are about carbon and nitrogen. Tea leaves are rich in nitrogen and hold water, so they act as greens whatever their colour.

items.p: A plant lives for years in a sealed jar. Explain how the leaves keep getting carbon dioxide.
items.a: Decomposers in the soil eat dead leaves and roots and breathe out carbon dioxide. The plant's own cells respire too. The leaves take that carbon dioxide in again in the light. The same carbon atoms go round inside the jar.
items.why: A strong answer names who makes the carbon dioxide and who uses it. It says that the atoms are used again, and only light comes in.

items.p: Which step sends nitrogen from the soil back into the air?
opts: Denitrifying, by bacteria in wet soil
items.why: Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen and give off nitrogen gas. Fixing goes the other way, from the air to the soil.

items.p: Heavy rain falls on a field just after too much urea is spread. Put what follows in order.
a: Rain washes nitrate into a lake
Algae multiply and the water turns green
The algae die and decomposers eat them
The decomposers use up the oxygen in the water
items.why: The spare nitrogen feeds algae first. The harm to fish comes later, when decomposers eating the dead algae use up the oxygen.
items: The decomposers use up the oxygen in the water
Rain washes nitrate into a lake
The algae die and decomposers eat them
Algae multiply and the water turns green

items.p: True or false: the carbon in your breath came from the food you ate.
items.why: True. Your cells take food apart for energy, and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. You do not get carbon from the air you breathe in.

items.p: Coal, oil and natural gas are called ____ fuels.
items.why: They formed from living beings who were buried for millions of years. A fossil is the remains of something that lived long ago.

items.p: Match each living being to their part in the nitrogen cycle.
items.why: Each step is done by a different kind of living being. If one kind were missing, the nitrogen would pile up at that step.
pairs: build protein from ammonium and nitrate
free nitrogen from dung and dead bodies
send nitrogen gas back to the air

items.p: Does each of these belong to the fast carbon cycle or the slow carbon cycle? Sort them.
items.why: The fast cycle runs through living beings in months or years. The slow cycle runs through rock and takes millions of years.
items: A leaf rots within a year
A volcano lets out carbon dioxide

items.p: Draw a legume root with nodules. Show what the plant gives the bacteria and what the bacteria give the plant.
items.a: A root with small round lumps on the sides. One arrow, labelled sugar, goes from the plant into a nodule. Another arrow, labelled nitrogen, goes from the nodule into the plant.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the trade in both directions. It may also show nitrogen gas coming from the air in the soil into the nodule.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Three of these put carbon into the air. Which one takes carbon out?
items.why: A growing forest takes in more carbon by photosynthesis than the forest gives out. Burning, rotting and breathing all give carbon dioxide to the air.

items.p: Soda water turns purple cabbage water pinker. What does that show about carbon dioxide?
items.why: Cabbage water turns pink with acid. Carbon dioxide joins with water to make a weak acid. The same thing happens, slowly, in the sea.

items.p: Should a small farm use factory fertiliser, or only compost? Three people disagree.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both the first two farmers are describing something real. Urea gives fast growth and big harvests, and it is easily lost to water and air. Compost builds the soil slowly, and there is rarely enough of it. Many will choose the scientist's plan and say why.
items.why: This is a real trade-off between a quick supply of nitrogen and the long-term health of the soil and water.

views.says: Urea gives my paddy nitrogen at once. Without it my harvest would be half.
Compost feeds the soil life and is not washed away so easily. My soil holds more water every year.
Roots take up the same nitrogen from both. Use compost, and add small doses of urea when the crop needs it.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose for a small farm? Give two reasons. Then say one thing that another person has right.

items.p: Label each kind of waste 'carbon-rich brown' or 'nitrogen-rich green': sawdust, grass cuttings, newspaper, banana peel.
items.why: Dry, woody waste is rich in carbon. Fresh, wet waste has more nitrogen. A bin needs about two parts of browns for one part of greens.
items.art: Four small drawings in a row, a heap of sawdust, grass cuttings, a newspaper and a banana peel, each with a blank box below.

items.p: Your breath has carbon dioxide in it. Explain why breathing does not make the air's carbon dioxide rise.
items.a: The carbon in my breath came from my food. The plants I ate took that carbon out of the air a few months earlier. So my breath only puts back what was taken out. Burning coal adds carbon that had been out of the air for millions of years.
items.why: A strong answer follows the carbon back to a plant and to the air. It says the difference between a loop and a one-way flow.

items.p: True or false: lightning fixes most of the nitrogen that plants use.
items.why: False. Lightning fixes a small share. Bacteria fix most of the nitrogen in nature, and today factories fix about as much again.

items.p: The round lumps on bean roots where bacteria fix nitrogen are called root ____.
items.why: The plant builds each nodule as a home for the bacteria and feeds them sugar.

worksheets.title: How We Know, and What People Changed (challenge)

items.p: Peas in clean sand grew well only when soil water was added. Why was boiled soil water tested too?
items.a: Boiling kills the bacteria in the soil water and leaves everything else in it. The peas given boiled soil water grew badly and made no nodules. So the living bacteria made the difference, and not something dissolved in the water.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two pots differed in only one thing, living bacteria. That is what makes the test fair.

items.p: The air's carbon dioxide went from 317 parts in a million to 427. About how much did it rise?
items.why: The rise is 427 − 317 = 110. One third of 317 is about 106. So the amount rose by about a third in 65 years.

items.p: Do living beings keep the Earth's air steady? Two scientists disagree.
items.a: A strong answer gives evidence for each. For the first: living beings made the oxygen in the air, and forests take up part of the extra carbon dioxide. For the second: long ago, bacteria filled the air with oxygen that poisoned many others, and today one kind of animal is changing the air fast.
items.why: Both agree that living beings shape the air. They disagree about whether anything holds it steady. Scientists still argue about this.

views.who: A scientist who supports the Gaia idea
views.says: All living beings together act as one system. When the air shifts, they respond in ways that bring it back.
Each bacterium takes what feeds them now. The cycles are a side effect, and nothing promises they will stay steady.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Give one piece of evidence for each view before you decide.

items.p: True or false: people now fix about as much nitrogen each year as nature does.
items.why: True. Fertiliser factories, engines and fields of legume crops together fix about as much as all the wild bacteria and lightning.

items.p: Put these stores of carbon in order, from the smallest to the largest.
items.why: Plants hold about half as much carbon as the air. Soil holds more than both together. The sea holds many times more, and rocks hold the most by far.

items.p: Is each of these a store or a flow? Sort them.
items.why: A store is an amount that stays somewhere. A flow is a movement from one store to another. A cycle needs both.
items: A leaf taking in carbon dioxide
The carbon in a coal seam
Rain washing nitrate into a river

items.p: The sharp-smelling gas that carries nitrogen out of a wet compost bin is ____.
items.why: When there is more nitrogen than the decomposers can use, the spare nitrogen leaves as ammonia gas.

items.p: Match each test to what it can show.
items.why: Each test changes or measures one thing. None of them alone shows a whole cycle, so scientists put many tests together.
pairs: Peas in sand, with and without soil water
Measuring mountain air for many years
whether carbon dioxide in the air is rising
that carbon dioxide makes water more acid
A plant in a sealed jar
that atoms can go round in a closed space

items.p: Draw the nitrogen cycle of a paddy field. Show one way nitrogen comes in and two ways it is lost.
items.a: Ways in: blue-green bacteria in the water, a dal crop with nodules, urea, compost or dung. Ways out: rain washing nitrate away, denitrifying bacteria in the wet mud, ammonia gas, and the harvested grain.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that a field is not closed. Nitrogen comes in and leaks out, and a farmer has to match the two.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Three of these take nitrogen away from a field. Which one adds nitrogen?
opts: Bacteria in the nodules of a dal crop
items.why: Bacteria in root nodules bring new nitrogen in from the air. The other three carry nitrogen out of the field.

items.p: Why is urea in India coated with neem oil?
opts: To slow bacteria who make nitrate
To give it a better smell
items.why: Nitrate is easily washed away. Neem slows the soil bacteria who make nitrate, so the nitrogen stays near the roots for longer.

items.p: In Carbon Journey, a six lets you leave the rock. What does the game get wrong about real rock?
items.a: In the game you leave the rock after a few throws. A real carbon atom can stay in rock for millions of years, far longer than in any other store. The game shows which stores are slow, but it cannot show how slow.
items.why: A strong answer says what the model shows well and what it leaves out. Every model leaves something out.

items.p: A model field loses fertiliser in rain. Label each part: food colour, cup with holes, dry leaves, run-off.
a: Dry leaves: mulch on the soil
Run-off: water flowing to a stream or lake
items.why: A model is useful only when each part stands for something real. A strong answer can also name one thing the model leaves out, such as roots.
items.art: A sloping plate of soil with coloured drops on it, a cup with holes above, dry leaves on the soil and a bowl below, with four blank label lines.

items.p: True or false: a planted tree locks carbon away for millions of years, as coal does.
items.why: False. A tree holds carbon for decades or a few centuries. When the tree rots or burns, the carbon goes back to the air.

items.p: Which is true of the cells in the body of a 40-year-old person?
items.why: The body is rebuilt all the time with atoms from food. Most cells are replaced within years. A few kinds, such as some nerve cells, last a lifetime.

quiz.p: A mango leaf falls and rots away. What happens to the atoms of the leaf?
opts: They move into air, soil and living beings
They stay in the leaf for ever
quiz.why: Decomposers take the leaf apart. The carbon goes mostly to the air as carbon dioxide, and the nitrogen goes to the soil. Atoms are not destroyed and do not turn into energy when something rots.

quiz.p: Which of these takes carbon out of the air?
quiz.why: Only photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air. Rotting, breathing and burning all put carbon dioxide in.

quiz.p: Coal is burnt at a power station. Where was its carbon before the coal formed?
opts: In ancient plants, and earlier in the air
quiz.why: Coal formed from plants buried hundreds of millions of years ago. Those plants took their carbon from the air by photosynthesis. Burning coal puts that old carbon back in the air.

quiz.p: Air is mostly nitrogen. Why do crops still go short of nitrogen?
opts: Plants cannot split the paired nitrogen atoms
Nitrogen gas is too heavy to reach leaves
The air has nitrogen only at night
quiz.why: In the air, nitrogen atoms are joined in very strong pairs. Plants have no enzyme to split them, so they depend on bacteria, lightning or fertiliser for nitrogen in a usable form.

quiz.p: Which of these can fix nitrogen from the air?
opts: Bacteria in the root nodules of legumes
quiz.why: Certain bacteria have the enzyme that splits nitrogen pairs. Legumes keep such bacteria in their root nodules. Earthworms and mushrooms help to break down dead matter, and they do not fix nitrogen.

quiz.p: A cow eats grass and passes urine onto the soil. Who frees that nitrogen for plants to use again?
quiz.why: Soil microbes change the nitrogen in urine and dung into ammonium and nitrate, which roots can take up. Rain only moves the nitrogen. It does not change its form.

quiz.p: In waterlogged soil, bacteria change nitrate into nitrogen gas. Where does that nitrogen go?
quiz.why: Denitrifying bacteria give off nitrogen gas, which goes back to the air. This closes the nitrogen cycle. Plant roots cannot take up nitrogen gas.

quiz.p: Which mix makes compost quickly, without a bad smell?
opts: About two parts browns to one part greens
quiz.why: Decomposers need carbon and nitrogen together, with air and water. Dry leaves alone have too little nitrogen. Wet peels alone pack down, lose their air and smell.

quiz.p: A heap of only fresh grass smells sharp, like ammonia. What is leaving the heap?
quiz.why: Ammonia is a gas of nitrogen and hydrogen. Fresh grass has more nitrogen than the decomposers can use, and the spare nitrogen escapes. Adding browns keeps it in the heap.

quiz.p: Carbon dioxide in the air has risen since 1960. What is the main cause?
quiz.why: Fossil fuels hold carbon that was out of the air for millions of years. Breath only returns carbon that plants took out a few months before, so it adds nothing new.

quiz.p: Rain washes spare nitrogen fertiliser from fields into a lake. What can follow?
opts: Algae multiply, and later fish may die
quiz.why: The nitrogen feeds algae, and the water turns green. When the algae die, decomposers eating them use up the oxygen in the water, and fish can die.

quiz.p: Which of these is a flow, not a store?
opts: The carbon in a coal seam
A leaf taking in carbon dioxide
The carbon dissolved in the sea
quiz.why: A store is an amount that stays somewhere. A flow is a movement between stores. A leaf taking in carbon dioxide moves carbon from the air into the plant.

applications: Farmers in the Cauvery delta sow black gram after paddy. Bacteria in the root nodules fix nitrogen from the air, so the crop needs little bought fertiliser.
Before sowing a legume, farmers coat the seed with a packet of the right bacteria, so that nodules form even in a field new to that crop.
Urea made in India is coated with neem oil, which slows the soil bacteria who would turn its nitrogen into easily lost nitrate.
Homes, flats and whole towns compost their wet waste in pots, pipes and bins, by layering greens with browns and letting air in.
A sewage treatment plant uses nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria, one after the other, to send the nitrogen in waste water back to the air.
Scientists measure carbon dioxide on Mauna Loa and at other stations every day, so that every country can see how the air is changing.
Doctors and scientists use the rare, heavier carbon left by bomb tests to find out how old the cells of a body are.

open_questions.q: Will the land and the sea keep taking up half of the carbon dioxide that people add to the air?
open_questions.why_open: Forests, soils and the sea take up about half today. Warmer water holds less gas, and warmer soil rots faster. Nobody knows how long the uptake will last.

open_questions.q: Can crops such as rice and wheat be given nitrogen-fixing partners of their own?
open_questions.why_open: A kind of maize from the hills of Oaxaca in Mexico feeds nitrogen-fixing bacteria in a slime on roots that grow above the ground. Scientists are trying to bring this to other crops, and nobody has done it yet.

open_questions.q: How much nitrogen is fixed in the open sea, and by whom?
open_questions.why_open: In 2024 scientists found a sea alga with a nitrogen-fixing part inside each cell, which nobody had known was possible. There may be more such fixers that have not been found.

open_questions.q: Does spreading crushed rock on fields really remove carbon dioxide from the air, and how much?
open_questions.why_open: The slow carbon cycle does this naturally over millions of years. Speeding it up is being tried on farms in India and elsewhere, and measuring the result is hard.

open_questions.q: How much carbon will frozen northern soils let out as they thaw?
open_questions.why_open: These soils hold dead plants that have been too cold to rot. As they thaw, decomposers begin to eat them. How fast, and how much gas they give off, is still being measured.

open_questions.q: Do living beings, taken all together, keep the Earth's air steady?
open_questions.why_open: Living beings make and use the gases of the air. Whether that steadies the air or only changes it has been argued about since the 1970s.

maths.problem: In Browns, Greens or Both, each bottle started at 12 cm. On day 17 the browns were at 11 cm, the greens at 5 cm and the mix at 8 cm. What fraction of its height did each bottle lose?
maths.answer: The browns lost one twelfth, the greens lost seven twelfths and the mix lost one third.
maths.explain: Take the last height from the first. The browns sank 12 − 11 = 1 cm, which is 1/12. The greens sank 12 − 5 = 7 cm, which is 7/12, a little more than half. The mix sank 12 − 8 = 4 cm, which is 4/12 = 1/3.
maths.context: This is about the experiment Browns, Greens or Both. There you fill three bottles with different waste and measure how far each one sinks. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: height of the waste in cm

maths.why_maths: The bottles might not start at exactly the same height in your test. A fraction of the starting height lets you compare them fairly.

maths.problem: A good compost mix has 2 tumblers of browns for every 1 tumbler of greens. A family makes 3 tumblers of greens a day. How many tumblers of browns do they need for a week?
maths.explain: Each tumbler of greens needs 2 tumblers of browns. So 3 tumblers of greens need 3 × 2 = 6 tumblers of browns a day. In a week that is 6 × 7 = 42 tumblers. This is why people who compost collect dry leaves by the sackful.
maths.context: This is about the experiment Browns, Greens or Both. There the mix of 2 parts browns to 1 part greens rotted without a bad smell.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells you how much of one thing goes with another. With it you can plan a bin of any size.

maths.problem: The label says 100 grams of toor dal has 22 grams of protein, and 100 grams of rice has 7 grams. About 16 of every 100 grams of protein is nitrogen. How much nitrogen is in 100 grams of each?
maths.answer: About 3.5 grams in the dal and about 1.1 grams in the rice.
maths.explain: For the dal: 22 × 16 ÷ 100 = 3.52 grams. For the rice: 7 × 16 ÷ 100 = 1.12 grams. The dal holds about three times as much nitrogen as the rice, because 22 ÷ 7 is a little more than 3.
maths.context: This is about the activity Protein Hunt. There you read the protein on food labels, because every protein has nitrogen in it.
maths.why_maths: No label tells you the nitrogen in a food. A percentage lets you work it out from the protein, which the label does give.

maths.problem: The carbon dioxide in the air rose by 9 from 1960 to 1970, and by 24 from 2010 to 2020. About how many times faster was the second rise?
maths.answer: Between two and three times faster. It was about 2.7 times.
maths.explain: Both rises took ten years, so you can compare them directly. 24 ÷ 9 = 2.67, which is about 2.7. So the amount of carbon dioxide in the air was rising more than two and a half times as fast as it did fifty years earlier.
maths.context: This is about the activity Read the Keeling Curve. There you plot real measurements of the carbon dioxide in the air from 1960 to 2025.
maths.why_maths: A line that bends upwards is hard to describe in words. Dividing one rise by another says exactly how much faster the change has become.

maths.problem: In Carbon Journey, a coin leaves Coal and Oil only on a 6. You throw once each for 30 coins. About how many leave? Under the people's rule they leave on a 3, 4, 5 or 6. About how many leave now?
maths.answer: About 5 coins under the first rule, and about 20 under the people's rule.
maths.explain: A die has 6 faces. Under the first rule 1 face in 6 lets a coin out, and 30 ÷ 6 = 5. Under the people's rule 4 faces in 6 let a coin out, and 30 × 4 ÷ 6 = 20. That is four times as many. Real throws will not give exactly these numbers, because a die is chance.
maths.context: This is about the game Carbon Journey. There you are a carbon atom, and a die decides when you leave each store.
maths.why_maths: Chance tells you what to expect from many throws, even though you cannot tell what one throw will give.

maths.problem: People add about 40 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide to the air each year. About half stays in the air. If people added only 20 billion tonnes, and the sea and land still took up 20 billion, how much would stay?
maths.answer: None. The amount in the air would stop rising.
maths.explain: Today 40 billion tonnes go in, and the sea and land take out about half, which is 20 billion. So 40 − 20 = 20 billion tonnes stay each year. If only 20 billion went in and 20 billion still came out, then 20 − 20 = 0. In real life the sea and land would slowly take up less, so this sum is only a first guess.
maths.context: This is about the activity Read the Keeling Curve. There you see that the carbon dioxide in the air is rising, because more flows in than flows out.
maths.why_maths: A store rises only when more flows in than flows out. Taking one flow from the other shows how much the flows must change before the rise stops.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that bacteria, and not plants, take nitrogen from the air? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: From 1836, the French scientist Jean-Baptiste Boussingault ran tests on a farm at Pechelbronn. He measured the nitrogen that went into the soil and the nitrogen that came out. After a crop of clover or peas, the soil held more nitrogen than before. Many people supposed that such plants took nitrogen straight from the air, as all plants take carbon. Boussingault tested that too, and his answer was no. Plants cannot use the nitrogen gas of the air. So where did the peas get it? The puzzle stood for fifty years. In 1886 two Germans, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth, grew peas in clean sand that held no nitrogen. The peas stayed small and died early. Then they added a little water that had run through ordinary field soil. Lumps formed on the roots, and the peas grew well. When they boiled the soil water first, no lumps formed and the peas failed. Something alive in the soil was living in the lumps and taking nitrogen from the air. Soon afterwards the Dutch scientist Martinus Beijerinck grew those bacteria by themselves.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean-Baptiste Boussingault in France, then Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth in Germany, and Martinus Beijerinck in the Netherlands
how_we_found_out.when: Boussingault's farm tests began in 1836. Hellriegel first reported the pea tests in Berlin in September 1886, and the full account was printed in 1888.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That plants of the bean family take nitrogen straight from the air by themselves. The pea tests showed that the plant alone cannot. Bacteria from the soil, living in the root nodules, do it.
how_we_found_out.art: A bearded scientist in a nineteenth-century glasshouse looking at two rows of glass pots of sand: in one row tall green pea plants, in the other small yellow ones.

roots.context: We have followed carbon and nitrogen atoms from the air into living beings and back. Now we ask what these two cycles tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Browns, Greens or Both, the bottle of damp leaves and paper hardly rotted. It was full of carbon, and it stood in air that is four-fifths nitrogen. But most decomposers cannot take nitrogen from the air, and dry leaves hold very little. So a living being can go short of something while surrounded by it. What matters is the form a thing is in, and who is able to change that form.
deep_truth.habit: We count how much of a thing there is, and call it plentiful or scarce. That leaves out the form the thing is in. The nitrogen of the air is plentiful and almost useless to a plant until a bacterium has changed it. Having a great deal of something near you is different from being able to use it.
deep_truth.evidence: The bottle of only browns stood in air that is nearly four-fifths nitrogen, and still rotted the slowest. In 1886, peas in clean sand starved in the open air until bacteria from the soil were added. Today nearly half of all people eat food grown with nitrogen that factories have fixed from the air.

three.who_am_i: The carbon in your body came out of the air through a leaf. The nitrogen in your muscles was taken from the air by a bacterium or a factory. You are built from air, by way of other living beings.
three.what_is_life: No living being makes their own atoms. Each one takes atoms that others have finished with, uses them for a while and passes them on.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has one fixed set of atoms and uses them again and again. What changes is the form they are in, and who can use them in that form.

roots.thread: The same carbon atoms are found in the air, a leaf, an idli, your arm and a sea shell. The same nitrogen atoms are found in the air, a root nodule, a dal seed and your hair. So the many things we see are a few kinds of atom, joined in different ways and handed from one being to the next. Every being who takes part senses and decides. A root lets the right bacteria in, and a bacterium swims towards a root. The cycles are what living beings do together.

teachings.teaching: The text follows what leaves a body at death. It becomes mist, then cloud, then rain. It falls to the earth and is born as grain, herbs, trees, sesame and beans. Whoever eats that food carries it on.
teachings.link: The Upanishad is speaking of the journey of a soul, not of atoms. But the path it describes is the path of a matter cycle: air, rain, plant, eater. Its authors had watched closely where a body goes.
verse: त इह व्रीहियवा ओषधिवनस्पतयस्तिलमासा इति जायन्ते

teachings.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 1.262 to 1.264
teachings.teaching: Nothing that we see is wholly lost. Nature remakes one thing out of another, and lets nothing be born unless the death of something else has helped.
teachings.link: Lucretius wrote this in Rome about two thousand years ago, long before anyone had seen a bacterium. Decomposers are the ones who do the remaking he describes.

teachings.teaching: Manuring does a field more good than ploughing. And once the weeding is done, guarding the crop does more good than watering.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar wrote for Tamil farmers well over a thousand years ago. Nobody then knew of nitrogen. The farmers had learned from their fields that what a crop takes from the soil must be given back.

science.text: Living beings do not make or destroy atoms. The same carbon and nitrogen atoms are used again and again.
In nature, only certain microbes can fix nitrogen from the air. Every plant and animal depends on them.
Whether living beings, all together, keep the Earth's air steady is still argued about.

other_view.who: Ford Doolittle, a Canadian biologist, writing in 1981, and many biologists since
other_view.view: There is no sharing and no plan in these cycles. Each bacterium takes what helps them to live now. What they leave behind happens to be useful to someone else. If the leftover were a poison, they would leave it just the same. Long ago, the oxygen made by blue-green bacteria poisoned many of the beings then alive.

practice.title: Follow one breath
practice.say: Sit still and breathe in slowly. Most of this breath is nitrogen. It goes into you and comes out again unchanged. Now breathe out slowly. In this breath is carbon from the food you ate today. Think of a leaf near your window taking that carbon in. Now rest a hand on your arm. The nitrogen in this muscle was in the air once. A bacterium or a factory brought it in. Take three more slow breaths.
practice.kid: Sit still. Breathe in slowly. Most of this breath is nitrogen. Breathe out slowly. This breath carries carbon from your food. Think of a leaf taking that carbon in. Rest a hand on your arm. That nitrogen was once in the air. Take three more slow breaths.

ask: A plant stands in nitrogen and still goes short of nitrogen. Is there something all around you that you cannot use yet? What would have to change?
Every atom in you was somewhere else before, and will be somewhere else later. So what is it that stays 'you'?
Bacteria fix nitrogen for every plant and animal. Are they helping the rest of us, or only living their own lives? Could both be true?
People now fix as much nitrogen as the rest of nature. Does that make us part of the cycle, or a break in the cycle?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged by a window breathing out, with a faint line from their breath to a leaf on a potted plant, and another from the soil in the pot to their arm.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. None of the experiments was tried at home for this lesson. They were reasoned through, and a parent should know the following. Browns, Greens or Both (core) runs for 17 days in three cut bottles. The greens should sink the most and turn wet and smelly within a week, the browns should hardly change, and the mix should sink steadily with a faint smell of earth. Keep the bottles on a balcony or an open window sill, under cloth, because the greens can smell strongly and draw fruit flies. The step says what to do if the smell is too strong. The test cannot separate 'tough' from 'short of nitrogen' as the reason for slow browns, and the unit says so. In Sour Air, the change from breath alone is small and depends on your water. Filtered drinking water and a side-by-side look on white paper help. Soda water always gives a clear change. Purple cabbage is not in every shop, so red hibiscus flowers are given as a second choice, and their colours differ. Bottle World can grow mould if the soil is too wet, and it must be kept out of direct sun. Root Dig needs a garden, park or farm and is outside the core path. Nodules are sometimes missing, and the step says what that means. Keep It in the Field is wet and muddy, so it is done in a bathroom or on a balcony.
